tabriz: Tabriz lies in the valley of the Quru River in Iran's historic Azerbaijan region, between the Sahand and Eynali mountains, at an elevation of between 1,350 and 1,600 metres. The valley opens into a plain that slopes gently down to the eastern shore of Lake Urmia, 60 kilometres to the west. The area is prone to earthquakes, and the city has been devastated and rebuilt several times; earthquakes are recorded in 858, 1041 and 1721. According to some sources the name derives from tap-riz, meaning flowing hot, in reference to the area's thermal springs.

Early history is poorly documented. An Iron Age graveyard of the first millennium BCE was found beside the Blue Mosque, and the city appears as Tarui or Tauris in an inscription of the Assyrian king Sargon II dated 714 BCE. After the Muslim conquest the Azd tribe from Yemen settled there. In 791 Zubaidah, wife of the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid, rebuilt the city after a devastating earthquake and beautified it so much that she was credited as its founder.

Tabriz was the capital of the Ilkhanate from 1265, and under Ghazan Khan, who came to power in 1295, it reached its highest splendour. It was again a capital under the Qara Qoyunlu from 1375 to 1468 and the Aq Qoyunlu from 1468 to 1500. Ismail I was crowned there in 1501 and announced Twelver Shia Islam as the official religion of the Safavid Empire, and the largely Sunni population was forced to convert. After the Battle of Chaldiran in 1514 Selim I sacked the city, and in 1555 Tahmasp I moved the capital to Qazvin to escape the growing Ottoman threat.

Its closeness to the West made Tabriz the centre of the Iranian Constitutional Revolution between 1905 and 1911, led locally by Sattar Khan and Bagher Khan. Russian forces occupied it in 1909 and again from December 1911, executing about 1,200 residents, and held it until 1917.

Tabriz is the capital of East Azerbaijan province and the largest economic centre of north-western Iran, with a population of over 1.7 million in 2016. Most of its people speak Iranian Azerbaijani as their first language and Persian as their second. Its Bazaar is a World Heritage Site, and most preserved monuments date from the Ilkhanid, Safavid and Qajar periods. The city is known for hand-woven carpets, and the University of Tabriz was established in 1947.
tacitus: Little is known of the personal life of Tacitus. What is known comes from scattered hints in his own works, the letters of his friend Pliny the Younger and an inscription found at Mylasa in Caria. He was born in 56 or 57 into an equestrian family. His place of birth and his first name are not known: the letters of Sidonius Apollinaris call him Gaius, and the major manuscript of his work gives Publius. His marriage to the daughter of a senator from Gallia Narbonensis suggests that he came from that province. He owed his rank to the Flavian emperors, as he says himself.

Tacitus studied rhetoric in Rome to prepare for a career in law and politics. In 77 or 78 he married Julia Agricola, daughter of the general Gnaeus Julius Agricola. He entered political life as a quaestor in 81 or 82 under Titus, became praetor in 88 and served in the provinces from about 89 to about 93. He gained acclaim as an orator, which sits ironically with his cognomen, Tacitus, meaning silent.

He and his property survived the reign of Domitian, but the experience left him jaded and perhaps ashamed of his own complicity, and instilled in him the hatred of tyranny evident in his works. In 97, under Nerva, he became suffect consul, the first of his family to do so. In 100 he and Pliny prosecuted Marius Priscus, proconsul of Africa, for corruption. In 112 to 113 he held the governorship of the province of Asia.

Five works ascribed to Tacitus survive, with gaps. The Life of Agricola and the Germania date to about 98. The Germania is an ethnographic work on the Germanic tribes outside the empire. The Dialogue on Oratory followed about 102, the Histories about 105 and the Annals about 117. The Histories and the Annals were meant to form a single work of thirty books, a continuous narrative from the death of Augustus in 14 to the death of Domitian in 96.

Of the Histories only the first four books and part of the fifth survive, covering the year 69 and part of 70. Of the Annals, books 7 to 10 and parts of others are missing. The first half survives in a single manuscript from Corvey Abbey and the second half in one from Monte Cassino.
tagalog-language: Tagalog is a Central Philippine language within the Austronesian family, and so related to Malagasy, Javanese, Indonesian, Malay and Tetum. It is closely related to the languages of the Bicol Region and the Visayas, including Waray, Hiligaynon and Cebuano. It differs from them in its treatment of the Proto-Philippine schwa vowel, which merged with one vowel in most Bikol and Visayan languages and with another in Tagalog. The word Tagalog is possibly derived from taga-ilog, meaning river dweller. The linguists David Zorc and Robert Blust speculate that the Tagalogs and other Central Philippine groups originated in northeastern Mindanao or the Eastern Visayas.

Before the Spanish arrived in 1521 and began colonisation in 1565, Tagalog was written in an abugida called Baybayin, with symbols for three vowels and 14 consonants. It belongs to the Brahmic family of scripts and is believed to descend from the script used by the Bugis in Sulawesi. It gradually gave way to the Latin alphabet taught by the Spaniards. Until the first half of the 20th century Tagalog was written in various ways based on Spanish orthography, in a 32-letter alphabet called the abecedario. In 1940 the grammarian Lope K. Santos introduced a 20-letter alphabet called the Abakada, and in 1971 the alphabet was expanded to make room for loans, especially Spanish and English family names.

Tagalog was declared the official language by the first revolutionary constitution of the Philippines, the Constitution of Biak-na-Bato, in 1897. The selection of a Tagalog-based national language in 1937 caused controversy, with speakers of Cebuano and Ilocano mainly regarding it as a cultural imposition. President Manuel L. Quezon signed Executive Order No. 263 in 1939, designating the language the Wikang Pambansâ, and on 12 April 1940 the teaching of the national language was ordered in all public and private schools. The first Tagalog Bible, Ang Biblia, was published in 1905.

Tagalog is spoken as a first language by the ethnic Tagalog people, a quarter of the population of the Philippines, and as a second language by the majority. Its standardised form, Filipino, is the national language and one of the two official languages with English. The Tagalog homeland, Katagalugan, covers much of central and southern Luzon, and Tagalog is also spoken natively on Marinduque and Mindoro.

The language commonly uses verb-subject-object order and is agglutinative, with verbs that take many prefixes, infixes and suffixes. Its vocabulary is mostly native Austronesian, with many Spanish and English loanwords and, from the precolonial use of Trade Malay, many Malay words. Words from Sanskrit, Tamil, Hokkien and other Chinese languages, Japanese, Arabic and Persian also appear. The polite particles pô and hô express respect to elders and others.
taipei: Taipei lies in northern Taiwan, mostly on the Taipei Basin, an ancient lakebed. The basin is bounded by the narrow valleys of the Keelung and Xindian rivers, which join to form the Tamsui River along the city's western border. The city is an enclave of the municipality of New Taipei City and sits about 25 kilometres southwest of the port city of Keelung. In the north the terrain rises to Qixing Mountain, 1,120 metres high, the highest dormant volcano in Taiwan, in Yangmingshan National Park.

The spellings Taipei and Tʻai-pei derive from the Wade–Giles romanisation, and the name means the north of Taiwan in Chinese. During Japanese rule from 1895 to 1945 the city was known as Taihoku, the Japanese reading of the same two characters.

Before the influx of Han Chinese colonists, the Taipei Basin was inhabited mainly by the Ketagalan, a Plains Indigenous people. The number of Han colonists grew gradually from the early 18th century under Qing rule, after the government began permitting development in the area. In 1875 the northern part of the island was incorporated into the new Taipeh Prefecture. Taipeh-fu was the temporary capital of the island in 1887, when it was declared a province, Fukien-Taiwan Province, and it was formally made the provincial capital in 1894.

When the Empire of Japan annexed Taiwan in 1895, the name was changed to Taihoku and the city was administered under Taihoku Prefecture. The Japanese rulers embarked on an extensive programme of urban planning that featured extensive railway links, and a number of landmarks and cultural institutions date from this period. The National Taiwan Museum, the island's oldest, was founded by the colonial government on 24 October 1908. Taipei has been the national seat of the central government of the Republic of China since 1949, and in 1967 it became a special municipality under the Executive Yuan.

Taipei is the capital of Taiwan, and the municipality had an estimated population of 2,494,813 in March 2023. It forms the core of the Taipei–Keelung metropolitan area, with New Taipei and Keelung, which has 7,047,559 inhabitants. The city is the political, economic, educational and cultural centre of Taiwan.

Its landmarks include the Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall, the Lungshan Temple of Manka, the Zhinan Temple, the National Palace Museum and the Presidential Office Building, around which stands Ketagalan Boulevard, a site of parades and public gatherings. Natural features include Maokong, Yangmingshan and hot springs. Because of the island's ambiguous political status, the name Chinese Taipei is used for Taiwan in international organisations and sporting events such as the Olympics.
taj-mahal: Shah Jahan, the fifth Mughal emperor, commissioned the Taj Mahal in 1631 as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died on 17 June that year giving birth to their 14th child. Court historians record that he avoided royal affairs for a week in his grief and for two years gave up music and lavish dress. He chose land south of Agra on which stood a mansion of Raja Jai Singh I, who agreed to give it in exchange for a large palace in the centre of the city.

Construction began in 1632. The mausoleum was completed in 1648 and the rest of the complex in 1653. More than 20,000 workers and artisans took part under a board of architects led by the court architect Ustad Ahmad Lahori. The white marble came from Makrana in Rajasthan, and 28 kinds of precious and semi-precious stone, from China, Tibet, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka and Arabia among other places, were inlaid in it.

The mausoleum stands on the right bank of the Yamuna at the centre of a complex of 17 hectares, with a mosque, a guest house and formal gardens enclosed by a crenellated red sandstone wall on three sides. It draws on Timurid and Mughal models, including the Gur-e Amir in Samarkand, the tomb of Timur, and Humayun's Tomb in Delhi, which inspired its charbagh garden.

The marble building stands on a square plinth with four identical sides, each with an iwan, a vaulted arched doorway, and is topped by an onion-shaped marble dome 23 metres high with a gilded finial. Shah Jahan himself was later buried beside his wife. The plan is symmetrical and aligned north to south, and the marble appears to change colour with the hour and the weather.

Shah Jahan, deposed by his son Aurangzeb in 1658, was held at Agra Fort, from where he could see the Taj Mahal, and died in 1666. By the late 19th century parts were in disrepair, and Lord Curzon ordered a restoration completed in 1908. The Archaeological Survey of India has maintained it since 1947.

UNESCO designated it a World Heritage Site in 1983 as the jewel of Muslim art in India and one of the universally admired masterpieces of the world's heritage. A longstanding story that he planned a black marble twin across the river comes from the writings of the traveller Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, and excavations in the 1990s showed that the blackened stones at Mehtab Bagh had been white.
tallahassee: Indigenous peoples occupied the Tallahassee area for thousands of years before European contact. Around 1200 the large and complex Mississippian culture built earthwork mounds near Lake Jackson, which survive today and are preserved in the Lake Jackson Archaeological State Park. The city covers 254.3 square kilometres, of which 247.9 are land, and lies in a humid subtropical climate with long summers and short, mild winters.

Florida became an American territory in September 1821, in accordance with the Adams-Onís Treaty of 1819, and Tallahassee became its capital in 1824. According to the city's heritage account, most of its original founders were settlers from North Carolina, descended from Scots or from Scots Presbyterians from County Down and County Antrim. Florida State University, founded in 1851, stands on the oldest continuous site of higher education in the state. Frenchtown is the oldest historically black neighbourhood in Florida.

Until the Second World War Tallahassee remained a small Southern town, with virtually the whole population within one mile of the Capitol. Its main economic drivers were the colleges and state government. The first plan to consolidate government buildings in one downtown area was the Taylor Plan of 1947, and in 1974 the Capitol Center Planning Commission produced a plan for expanding the centre, projecting 2.3 million square feet of new government facilities. In the Jim Crow period, laws passed by Democrats in Florida disenfranchised most African Americans until the late 1960s, which kept the Republican Party uncompetitive in the area for decades.

Tallahassee is the capital of Florida, the county seat of Leon County and its only incorporated municipality, with 196,169 residents at the 2020 census. It holds the Florida State Capitol, the Supreme Court of Florida and the Governor's Mansion, and is a college town, home to Florida State University, Florida A&M University and Tallahassee State College. Its museums include the Museum of Florida History, the Old Capitol Museum, the Knott House Museum and Mission San Luis de Apalachee.
talmud: Talmudic tradition emerged and was compiled between the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE and the Arab conquest in the early seventh century. In antiquity the two major centres of Jewish scholarship were the academies of Syria Palaestina and of Babylonia, and each produced a Talmud. The earlier, the Jerusalem Talmud, was compiled in Galilee between the late fourth century and the first half of the fifth. It is also called the Palestinian Talmud, which is more accurate, since it was not compiled in Jerusalem, and it draws on the teachings of rabbis at Tiberias, Sepphoris and Caesarea.

The Babylonian Talmud consists of documents compiled over late antiquity, from the 3rd to the 6th centuries. Babylonian centres of learning included Nehardea, Nisibis, Mahoza, Pumbedita and the Sura Academy. Tradition holds that Rav Ashi and Ravina II compiled it around 500 CE, but it is more likely to have been compiled in the middle of the sixth century.

The Talmud follows the structure of the Mishnah, a compilation of legal opinions and debates by the Tannaim, rabbis of the second century CE. It is divided into six orders, abbreviated as Shas, and 63 tractates, with 517 chapters in all. The Gemara is a commentary on the Mishnah, produced by the Amoraim, rabbis of the third to fifth centuries, through a process of debate called shakla v'tarya, or taking and throwing. It also comments on baraitot, traditions of the Oral Torah that are not in the Mishnah. Short later treatises, the minor tractates, are printed at the end of the order of damages.

The Babylonian Talmud is much longer, at about 2.5 million words, and a third of its material is non-legal Aggadah, against a sixth in the Jerusalem Talmud. It is written mostly in Jewish Babylonian Aramaic, with quotations of the Mishnah, baraitot and Hebrew scripture in Hebrew. The Jerusalem Talmud is written in a Western Aramaic dialect and is more fragmentary because its redaction was incomplete.

The only complete manuscript of the Talmud, Munich Codex Hebraica 95, dates from 1342. The earliest manuscript fragments, from the Cairo Genizah, date from the late seventh or eighth century, and Ms. Oxford 2673, with much of tractate Keritot, is the earliest manuscript with a known date, 1123.

Until the Haskalah of the 18th and 19th centuries the Talmud was the centrepiece of Jewish culture in nearly all communities and served as the guide for daily life. The word Talmud means study or learning, from the Semitic root lmd. When used without qualification it refers to the Babylonian Talmud, which has received far more attention from commentators and is held to be the more authoritative.
tamil-nadu: Tamil Nadu covers 130,058 square kilometres on the southeastern coast of the Indian peninsula. The Western Ghats and the Deccan Plateau lie to the west, the Eastern Ghats to the north and the Bay of Bengal to the east, with the Gulf of Mannar and the Palk Strait to the southeast and the Laccadive Sea at the southern cape. The river Kaveri crosses the state. The name means the land of the Tamils.

Excavations at Keezhadi have revealed a large urban settlement, with the earliest artefact dated to 580 BCE. Inscriptions at Adichanallur use Tamil Brahmi, dated to the 5th century BCE. In the Sangam period, from about 500 BCE to 300 CE, Tamilakam was ruled by three monarchical states: the Cheras in the west, the Pandyas in the south and the Cholas in the Kaveri delta. Their kings patronised the Vedic religion, Buddhism and Jainism and sponsored some of the earliest Tamil literature. The oldest surviving work is the Tolkāppiyam, a Tamil grammar.

The Pallavas, with Kanchipuram as their capital, were noted for their patronage of architecture, and the gopuram, the tower at the entrance of a temple, originated with them. They built the rock-cut monuments of Mahabalipuram and temples at Kanchipuram, and were in constant conflict with the Cholas and Pandyas until the Chola prince Aditya I defeated them in the 9th century. The Vijayanagara kingdom, founded in 1336, conquered the entire Tamil country by about 1370 and ruled for almost two centuries, until its defeat at the Battle of Talikota in 1565. Its military governors, the Nayaks of Madurai and Thanjavur, then took control and rebuilt temples such as the Meenakshi Temple at Madurai.

European colonisation began with trading ports in the 17th century, and the British controlled much of the state as part of the Madras Presidency for two centuries. After 1947 it became Madras State, which lost Andhra in 1953 and took its present shape when states were redrawn on linguistic lines in 1956. It was renamed Tamil Nadu on 14 January 1969.

Tamil Nadu is the southernmost state of India, with its capital at Chennai, and 72.1 million people at the census of 2011. Tamil, the first language recognised as classical in India, is its official language, and 87.6 per cent of its people follow Hinduism. It has four World Heritage Sites and is known for its great temples and its classical Tamil literature.
tampere: Tampere lies in the Finnish Lakeland, between Lake Näsijärvi and Lake Pyhäjärvi, which differ in water level by 18 m. The Tammerkoski rapids that connect them have been an important source of power throughout history, most recently for generating electricity. The Pyynikki Ridge, a large esker formed from moraine during the Weichselian glaciation, rises 160 m above sea level. The name derives from the rapids, and the explanation most accepted traces it to a Proto-Samic phrase for a deep, slow part of a stream followed by the word for rapids.

The earliest known permanent settlements around Tammerkoski date from the 7th century, when settlers from the west began to farm land in an area largely inhabited by Tavastian tribes. The population stayed small for centuries, and in 1638 Governor-General Per Brahe the Younger ordered two markets a year at Tammerkoski. The first industries in the 17th century were watermills and sawmills.

The neighbouring parish of Pirkkala had been the most important parish in the area through the Middle Ages. In 1771 and 1772 the pastor Erik Edner proposed a town on the banks of the rapids, Gustav III of Sweden made it a market town, and on 1 October 1779 Tampere received full town rights. Farming was forbidden within the city limits, so its inhabitants lived mainly by trade and crafts, and when the Grand Duchy of Finland was formed in 1809 the town still had fewer than a thousand inhabitants.

Tampere became known as the Manchester of the North for its past as a centre of Finnish industry, and the red-brick factories along the Tammerkoski, such as Finlayson and Tampella, left a strong mark on the city. It was also the scene of political events in the early 20th century. In 1905 the conference of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party, led by Vladimir Lenin, met in the Tampere Workers' Hall and decided to launch an armed insurrection. On 1 November 1905, during the General Strike, the Red Declaration was proclaimed in Keskustori.

Tampere is the regional capital of Pirkanmaa and the most populous inland city in the Nordic countries, with about 263,000 inhabitants. Finnish is the first language of most of them. Its buildings range from the Old Stone Church of Messukylä, the only medieval one, to Tampere Cathedral. Pispala, a ridge between the two lakes, housed much of the industrial labour in the late 19th and early 20th centuries and joined the city in 1937.
tang-dynasty: The Tang dynasty was founded by Emperor Gaozu, born Li Yuan, who had been Duke of Tang and governor of Taiyuan during the collapse of the Sui dynasty. The Li family were of ethnic Han origin and belonged to the north-western military aristocracy; Gaozu's mother was part Xianbei. Official Tang records trace the family's descent from Laozi, and Li Yuan used the claim to attract a following. The Tang took advantage of Sui decline and precipitated its final collapse in 618, and the first half of the dynasty was a period of progress and stability. The territory won by the military campaigns of its early rulers surpassed that of the Han dynasty.

The dynasty was formally interrupted from 690 to 705, when Empress Wu Zetian seized the throne and proclaimed the Wu Zhou dynasty, becoming the only legitimate Chinese female emperor. Emperor Xuanzong, who reigned from 712 to 756, ruled when the dynasty was at the height of its power.

The An Lushan rebellion of 755–763 ended its prosperity: An Lushan, a Tang commander, rebelled in Hebei with more than 100,000 troops, took Luoyang and named himself emperor of a new Yan state, and the court fled Chang'an. The Uyghur Khaganate helped recapture the capital, but demanded an enormous tribute in silk, and the Tang were never again able to reconquer Central Asia.

Regional military governors, the jiedushi, rose in the ninth century and weakened civil order. In the 840s Emperor Wuzong suppressed Buddhism. The rebellion of Huang Chao from 874 to 884 devastated northern and southern China and sacked both Chang'an and Luoyang; the Tang never recovered, and the dynasty ended in 907. It was followed by the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period.

The dynasty kept a civil service recruited by examinations and recommendations. Emperor Taizong issued a legal code that later Chinese dynasties and neighbouring polities in Vietnam, Korea and Japan took as a model; the earliest surviving code, of 653, has 500 articles. Candidates sat the mingjing, on the Confucian classics, or the jinshi, which tested essays and poetry. An official census of 609 counted about 50 million people.

By 742 the armies had about 500,000 men, and in 668 Tang and Silla forces destroyed the kingdom of Goguryeo. Chang'an, the capital, was laid out in 108 walled wards, and its checkerboard plan was copied in Heian-kyō. Over 48,900 Tang poems by more than 2,200 authors survive, among them those of Li Bai and Du Fu, and woodblock printing produced the Diamond Sutra of 868, the first full-length book printed at regular size.
tangier: Tangier lies in north-western Morocco, on the Mediterranean and the Atlantic. The centre sits about 23 kilometres east of Cape Spartel between two hills at the north-west end of the Bay of Tangier, so that the city rises like an amphitheatre with the commercial district in the middle. The western hill holds the citadel, or kasbah, and the eastern hill forms Cape Malabata. The bay was historically the best natural harbour on the Moroccan coast. The old Berber name Tingi is linked to a word for marsh, and the Greeks claimed that the city was named for Tinjis, a daughter of the Titan Atlas.

Tangier was founded as a Phoenician colony, possibly as early as the 10th century BCE and almost certainly by the 8th century BCE. Berber tombs around it held Punic jewellery by the 6th century BCE, and the Carthaginians made it an important port by the 5th. It probably took part in the expeditions of Hanno the Navigator. Vandals under Gaiseric occupied Tingis in 429 CE, and Belisarius reconquered it in 533 for Justinian I, although the provincial administration moved to Septem, now Ceuta.

The Portuguese failed to take Tangier in 1437, 1458 and 1464 but occupied it unopposed on 28 August 1471, after its garrison fled on learning that Asilah had fallen. They turned the chief mosque into a cathedral and built houses, chapels and monasteries. The Wattasids attacked in 1508, 1511 and 1515 without success. In the 17th century it passed with Portugal's other domains into Spanish control while keeping a Portuguese garrison. The United States opened its first consulate there, and in 1821 Slimane of Morocco gave the United States a mansion, now the Tangier American Legation Museum. The French under the Prince of Joinville bombarded Tangier on 6 August 1844.

In 1923 Tangier became an international zone managed by colonial powers, attracting diplomats, spies, writers and businessmen. Its legal status let nationalists meet there, and in 1951 the National Front, a pact of four nationalist parties, was created in Tangier. The powers agreed in 1952 to abolish the zone, and Tangier rejoined Morocco on the restoration of full sovereignty in 1956, with phases lasting to 1960. It is the capital of the Tangier-Tetouan-Al Hoceima region and a major industrial centre. Its economy has benefited from the Tanger-Med port.
tank: The tank is the 20th-century realisation of an ancient concept, that of giving troops mobile protection and firepower. At the Battle of Mobei in 119 BCE the Han general Wei Qing used armoured heavy wagons, drawn up in rings, to shelter archers, crossbowmen and infantry from the Xiongnu cavalry. In the 15th century Jan Žižka built armoured wagons carrying cannon, used effectively in several battles of the Hussite wars. The internal combustion engine, armour plate and the continuous track were the key innovations leading to the modern tank.

The word tank was first applied in a military context in 1915 to keep the nature of the British landships secret. According to Albert Gerald Stern, secretary of the Landship Committee, at a conference on 24 December 1915 Thomas J. Macnamara suggested changing the committee's title for secrecy, and Mr d'Eyncourt proposed water carriers. Stern, who thought the initials of that title unsuitable, changed the word to tank, and the committee became the Tank Supply Committee. In France Colonel J. B. E. Estienne had the word char d'assaut preferred.

A tank is an armoured fighting vehicle meant as a primary offensive weapon in front-line ground combat. Its capability rests on firepower, protection and mobility, and designs differ in how they blend them. In the First World War the first designs, such as the British Mark I, were long and large in order to cross wide trenches and were classed as heavy tanks, while smaller vehicles such as the French Renault FT were classed as light tanks or tankettes. Improved suspension in the Second World War, such as the Christie system and the torsion-bar suspension of Ferdinand Porsche, greatly improved cross-country performance. Japan was the first to begin moving from petrol to diesel engines, with the Type 89B in 1934.

The British and French built thousands of tanks in the First World War, while Germany, unconvinced of their potential and short of resources, built only twenty. Commanding tanks in the field was difficult. Armoured bulkheads, engine noise, dust and smoke hindered communication, and radios were not portable or robust enough to be mounted in a tank, although Morse code transmitters were installed in some Mark IVs at Cambrai as messaging vehicles. Crews sometimes sent reports back by releasing carrier pigeons, and vehicles signalled to one another by hand or by semaphore flags, which the Red Army and Soviet Army kept in use through the Second World War and the Cold War.
taoism: The core of Taoist thought crystallised during the early Warring States period, c. 450 to c. 300 BCE, when the Tao Te Ching and the Zhuangzi, widely regarded as the fundamental texts of Taoist philosophy, were largely compiled. Early Taoism drew on diverse influences, among them the Shang and Zhou state religions, Mohism, Confucianism and Legalist theories. Scholars disagree about its beginnings: Harold Roth argues that it began as inner-cultivation lineages of master and disciple, while Russell Kirkland holds that before the Han dynasty there were no real Taoists or Taoism, only sets of practices and ideas that were later synthesised.

By the Han dynasty, 202 BCE to 220 CE, the sources had coalesced into a coherent tradition of ritualists in the state of Shu, modern Sichuan. The Huang–Lao movement of the 2nd century BCE was an influential school, and the earliest surviving commentaries on the Tao Te Ching date from the Han. Taoist secret societies precipitated the Yellow Turban Rebellion in the late Han, attempting to create what has been characterised as a Taoist theocracy.

Taoism is a philosophical and religious tradition indigenous to China, emphasising harmony with the Tao, translated as way, road, path or technique. The opening line of the Tao Te Ching, that the Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao, is generally read to mean that the Tao is on an ultimate level indescribable. De, often translated virtue or power, is the active expression of the Tao, and the central values include ziran, naturalness, and wu wei, effortless action or non-interference. A common goal of practice is self-cultivation, which in religious forms includes longevity and immortality.

Religious Taoism has its own scriptures, priestly lineages, rites and ritual systems, and it has long been intertwined with Chinese folk religion, so that the boundary is often blurred. Its practices include offerings, the recitation of scriptures, purification rites, divination, meditation, and longevity methods related to Chinese medicine.

Monks assembled the Daozang canon from the 5th century CE onward. The alchemist Ge Hong wrote the Baopuzi in the 4th century. A united Taoist identity, called daojiao, gained official status in the Tang dynasty, which was the height of Taoist influence. Taoism was combined with Confucianism and Buddhism in the Three Teachings discourse by the 6th century. In the 19th and 20th centuries it suffered much destruction from persecution and wars, and by the 20th century only one complete copy of the Daozang survived intact, at the White Cloud Monastery in Beijing. It recovered after 1979, with temples restored and Taoist literature published.
taras-shevchenko: Taras Shevchenko was born on 9 March 1814 (25 February in the old style) in Morintsy, a village in Kiev Governorate, about 20 years after the third partition of Poland brought the territory under Russian rule. His parents were serf peasants who worked land owned by Vasily Engelhardt. When Engelhardt died in 1828, his son Pavel became the family's landlord and trained the 14-year-old Taras as a servant. In 1829 Taras travelled in Engelhardt's retinue to Warsaw and Vilno. When Engelhardt caught him painting a portrait of the Cossack general Matvei Platov at night, he had the boy whipped, but later apprenticed him to a painter-decorator, who recommended lessons from the Polish painter Franciszek Ksawery Lampi.

In Saint Petersburg the young Ukrainian artist Ivan Soshenko gave Shevchenko lessons and introduced him around June 1832 to the painter Karl Briullov. Briullov asked Engelhardt for Shevchenko's freedom and was refused. Shevchenko later became a student of the Imperial Academy of Arts with Briullov as his mentor. He travelled to Ukraine in 1843, 1845 and 1846, and in October 1843 wrote the poem The Dug Grave. In 1845 he became a drawing teacher at Kiev University and met members of the Brotherhood of Saints Cyril and Methodius.

He was arrested on 5 April 1847 and exiled to Central Asia for his association with the Brotherhood; he continued to create art and poetry despite prohibitions. He received an amnesty from the new emperor in 1857 but was not permitted to settle in Saint Petersburg until 1858. In June 1859 he visited Ukraine for the last time.

Shevchenko composed his last poem, left unfinished, on 14 February 1861 and died in Saint Petersburg on 10 March 1861. His friends carried out the wish he expressed in his poem Testament: his remains were taken to Ukraine, and on 22 May 1861 he was reburied on Monk's Hill, now Taras Hill, in Kaniv. Of 237 poems he wrote, only 28 were published in the Russian Empire during his life. He wrote his poetry in Ukrainian and his prose in Russian. His poetry, above all the Kobzar, is regarded as the foundation of modern Ukrainian literature.
tartu: Tartu lies about 186 kilometres southeast of Tallinn on the Emajõgi river, which connects Lake Võrtsjärv with Lake Peipus. Archaeological evidence of permanent settlement on the site dates to as early as the 5th century CE. By the 7th century local inhabitants had built a wooden fortification on the east side of Toome Hill, and around the 9th and 10th centuries the settlement became an inland trading centre. The name is thought to derive from the Estonian word for aurochs, tarvas.

From the 13th century until the end of the 19th, the town was known in most of the world by variants of Dorpat. In 1262 the army of Prince Dmitri of Pereslavl captured and destroyed it but could not take the bishop's fortress on Toome Hill. In the 1280s Dorpat joined the Hanseatic League. In 1558 Tsar Ivan the Terrible began the Livonian War by besieging it, and the local bishop was imprisoned in Moscow, which ended local self-government. The city then passed between the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and Sweden, which held it for good from 1625.

In 1708 Russian forces blew up the remaining fortifications and houses and deported the citizens to Russia, and with the Treaty of Nystad in 1721 the city became part of the Russian Empire. The Great Fire of 1775 destroyed most of the buildings in the centre, and the town hall was built between 1782 and 1789. In the second half of the 19th century Tartu was the cultural centre of the Estonians: it hosted the first song festival in 1869, the founding of the Vanemuine theatre in 1870 and of the Society of Estonian Literati in 1872. Much of the city was destroyed in the Second World War, and under Soviet rule the population almost doubled from 57,000 to over 100,000 between 1944 and 1991.

Tartu is often called the intellectual capital of Estonia. It is the seat of the Supreme Court of Estonia, the Estonian National Museum, whose new main building opened in 2016, and the Vanemuine theatre, the oldest Estonian-language theatre, and it is the birthplace of the Estonian Song Festivals. After independence was regained in 1991 the old town was renovated and St. John's Church, in ruins since the war, was restored.
tashkent: Tashkent is in northeastern Uzbekistan, on a well-watered plain on the road between Samarkand and Shymkent, just across the border in Kazakhstan. It sits at the confluence of the Chirchiq River and several of its tributaries and is built on deep alluvial deposits up to 15 m deep. The city lies in an active tectonic area and suffers numerous tremors and occasional earthquakes. Its climate is Mediterranean with some humid continental influences: winters are cold and often snowy, and summers are long, hot and dry.

Abu Rayhan Biruni wrote that the name comes from the Turkic tash and the Persian kent, Stone City or City of Stones. The older name Chach has been traced by Ilya Gershevitch to an Old Iranian word for an area of water or lake, though Ünal criticizes that derivation as based on too many assumptions and derives Čač from a Proto-Turkic word for stone.

Tashkent's history stretches back centuries as part of the ancient Silk Road. Before the influence of Islam in the mid-8th century, Sogdian and Turkic culture was predominant. Genghis Khan destroyed the city in 1219, after which it was rebuilt and profited from its place on the Silk Road. From the 18th to the 19th centuries it was an independent city-state, before being re-conquered by the Khanate of Kokand. The Russian Empire took Tashkent in 1865, and it became the capital of Russian Turkestan. In 1868 the Samarkand Kufic Quran was taken as a war trophy from Samarkand to Saint Petersburg, and the Bolsheviks returned it to Tashkent in 1923.

In Soviet times the city grew greatly and its population changed because of forced deportations from throughout the Soviet Union. Thousands of Pontic Greeks were displaced in the early 1940s, and about 11,000 refugees of the Greek Civil War were sent to Tashkent after 1949. Its population was 1,902,000 in 1983 and about 2,136,600 in 1991. The 1966 earthquake destroyed much of the city, which was rebuilt as a model Soviet city and was then the fourth-largest in the Soviet Union, after Moscow, Leningrad and Kiev. The Tashkent Metro, the first in Central Asia, opened in 1977.

Tashkent is the most populous city in Central Asia. Ethnic Uzbeks form the majority, and Uzbek is the main language, with Russian used as a lingua franca. Most of the ancient city was destroyed in the 1917 revolution and the 1966 earthquake. Surviving landmarks include the Kukeldash Madrasah, dating from the reign of Abdullah Khan II (1557-1598), Chorsu Bazaar, the Hazrati Imam Complex and the mausoleum of Qaffol Shoshi, built in 1542. The city marked 2,200 years of written history in 2009.
tatars: The name Tatar possibly referred first to the Tatar confederation, which Genghis Khan incorporated into the Mongol Empire. Western cartographers later applied the term, often spelled Tartar, to anyone from the northern and central Asian landmass then known as Tartary. The name became that of populations of the former Golden Horde in Europe, such as those of the Kazan, Crimean, Astrakhan, Qasim and Siberian Khanates. The Persian word is first recorded in the 13th century in reference to the hordes of Genghis Khan. Studies of ancestry suggest that the three main groups, the Volga, Crimean and Siberian Tatars, formed independently of one another.

The Volga Tatars descend from Kipchaks of the Golden Horde or from Volga Bulgars who survived the Mongol conquest of 1236 to 1237. About 40 thousand Tatars arrived with Khan Uluk-Muhammad in 1438 to 1445 when the Kazan Khanate was formed. Its conquest by Ivan IV in 1552 followed a six-month siege.

The Crimean Tatars formed between the 13th and 17th centuries, mainly from Kipchaks and Ottoman Turks. Crimea passed to the Giray dynasty, founded by Hacı Giray after an embassy invited him from Lithuania in 1441.

In 1502 the Crimean Khanate defeated the Great Horde, and it was among the strongest powers in Eastern Europe until the early 18th century, formally a vassal of the Ottoman Empire. A major source of income was frequent raids into Eastern Europe and the Caucasus for slaves.

Russia annexed it in 1783, and at least 800 thousand Tatars left Crimea by the early 20th century. In May 1944 the Soviet State Defense Committee ordered the deportation of all Crimean Tatars to Central Asia, and 46 per cent of them are said to have died during the deportation and the first years of exile.

Tatars settled in the Polish-Lithuanian lands between the 13th and 17th centuries. The Lipka Tatars first settled in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania at the beginning of the 14th century, and Grand Duke Vytautas invited a further, Muslim wave towards the end of it. The grand dukes encouraged the migrations because of the Tatars' reputation as skilled warriors, and the settlers were granted szlachta (noble) status. Estimates for the 17th century put their number at about 15,000, in about 60 villages with mosques.

They kept their religion and culture through royal privileges and internal autonomy, and were allowed to marry Christians, which was uncommon in Europe at the time. By the 18th century they had adopted the local language. The May Constitution of 1791 gave them a seat in the Sejm. Henryk Sienkiewicz's historical novels made their role well known in Poland.
tatarstan: Tatarstan lies in the centre of the East European Plain, about 800 kilometres east of Moscow, between the Volga and the Kama rivers. It covers 68,000 square kilometres and borders Kirov, Ulyanovsk, Samara and Orenburg oblasts and the republics of Mari El, Udmurtia, Chuvashia and Bashkortostan. Its capital and largest city is Kazan. Oil, natural gas and gypsum are its main natural resources.

The earliest known organised state within its present boundaries was Volga Bulgaria (c. 700 to 1238), a mercantile state with trade contacts across Inner Eurasia, the Middle East and the Baltic. Islam was introduced by missionaries from Baghdad around the time of Ibn Fadlan's journey in 922. The Golden Horde and the Khanate of Kazan followed, until Russia conquered the khanate in 1552. In the 19th century the region became a centre of Jadidism, an Islamic movement that preached tolerance of other religions.

During the Civil War of 1918 to 1920 Tatar nationalists tried to found an independent Idel-Ural State with the neighbouring Bashkirs. The Bolsheviks, who had at first supported it, arrested members of its parliament in March 1918. The Tatar Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic was established on 27 May 1920, with boundaries that did not include a majority of the Volga Tatars. On 30 August 1990 Tatarstan declared its sovereignty. A constitution approved by about 62 per cent of voters in 1992 defined it as a sovereign state, but the Russian Constitutional Court declared the referendum and constitution unconstitutional. Since the 2002 text, the constitution defines Tatarstan as part of the Russian Federation.

Tatarstan is a republic of the Russian Federation. Its two state languages are Tatar and Russian, and the official script is Cyrillic. The 2021 census counted 4,004,809 inhabitants, among them about 2 million Tatars and 1.5 million Russians, with Chuvash, Mari and Udmurts in smaller numbers. Most Tatars are Sunni Muslims, and a minority, the Keräşen Tatars, are Orthodox Christians. Three UNESCO World Heritage Sites lie in the republic: the Kazan Kremlin, the Bulgarian State Museum-Reserve, and the Assumption Cathedral and Monastery of the town-island of Sviyazhsk.
tbilisi: Tbilisi stands on the banks of the Kura River. Its name comes from the Old Georgian tpili, meaning warm, because of the area's numerous sulfuric hot springs. Until 1936 the name in English and most other languages followed the Persian pronunciation, Tiflis. On 17 August 1936, by order of the Soviet leadership, the official Russian names of various cities were changed to match the local language, and the Georgian form was modernised from Ṭpilisi to Tbilisi on the proposal of Georgian linguists. Some languages, among them Turkish, Persian, Greek, Spanish and German, have kept a form of Tiflis. Its position at the crossroads between Europe and Asia, near the Silk Road, made it a point of contention among powers.

Archaeologists found evidence of continuous habitation of the suburb of Dighomi since the early Bronze Age, and stone artifacts from the Paleolithic. In the late Bronze Age and early Iron Age it was the largest settlement in the Caucasus. According to legend the site was covered by forest as late as 458. One widely accepted variant of the foundation myth says that King Vakhtang I of Iberia (r. c. 447/49 - 502/22) went hunting with a falcon, which caught or injured a pheasant, and both birds fell into a hot spring and died of burns. The king was so impressed by the springs that he had the forest cleared and built a city there.

King Dachi of Iberia (r. 522-534), Vakhtang's successor, moved the capital of Iberia from Mtskheta to Tbilisi and began building the fortress wall that marked the city's new boundaries. From the sixth century Tbilisi grew steadily because of its strategic position on trade and travel routes between Europe and Asia. It served as the capital of various Georgian kingdoms and republics.

Between 1801 and 1917, as part of the Russian Empire, it was the seat of the Caucasus Viceroyalty, which governed both the northern and southern sides of the Caucasus. Its population has always been diverse in culture, ethnicity and religion, though overwhelmingly Eastern Orthodox Christian.

Tbilisi is the capital and largest city of Georgia, with more than 1.3 million inhabitants, almost one third of the country's population. Its architecture mixes medieval, neoclassical, Beaux Arts, Art Nouveau, Stalinist and modern buildings. Among its landmarks are the Sameba and Sioni cathedrals, the medieval Narikala Fortress and the Georgian National Museum.
tegucigalpa: Tegucigalpa lies in the southern-central highlands of Honduras, in a valley ringed by mountains, in the department of Francisco Morazán, of which it is also the departmental capital. The city stands on a chain of mountains, at elevations of 975 metres at its lowest points and 1,463 metres in its highest suburbs, and is hilly with few flat areas. The Choluteca River separates it from its sister city Comayagüela. The surrounding country was open woodland of pine and oak, and the climate is a tropical savanna one, tempered by the altitude, with a rainy and a dry season.

The Spaniards claimed the site on 29 September 1578 and founded it as the Real de Minas de San Miguel de Tegucigalpa, on the site of an existing settlement of the Lenca and the Tolupans. Juan de la Cueva became its first mayor in 1579. Among its first important buildings were the Dolores Church (1735), the San Miguel Cathedral (1765), the Casa de la Moneda (1780) and the Immaculate Conception Church (1788). The origin of the name is uncertain: the most widely accepted version derives it from a Nahuatl phrase meaning 'hills of silver', although the local people are said to have been unaware of the mineral deposits, and other proposals include 'painted rocks'.

On 30 October 1880 President Marco Aurelio Soto moved the seat of government from Comayagua to Tegucigalpa. The constitution of 1936 made Tegucigalpa and Comayagüela a single Central District, formed on 30 January 1937, and the constitution of 1982 keeps that arrangement as the permanent national capital. In late October and early November 1998 Hurricane Mitch stayed over Honduras for five days; on saturated ground and deforested slopes the rain caused catastrophic flooding, especially in Tegucigalpa, and destroyed parts of the city along the banks of the Choluteca.

Tegucigalpa is the largest city of Honduras and its political and administrative centre, seat of the national government and of the National Autonomous University of Honduras, founded in 1847. Legally the capital is the Municipality of the Central District, though nearly all government institutions stand on the Tegucigalpa side of the river, while Comayagüela on the western bank is largely made up of lower-income neighbourhoods. The census of 2013 counted 1,157,509 people in the Central District. Roman Catholicism has been the leading religion since the Mercedarian missions of about 1548, and the Diocese of Comayagua was moved to the city and renamed the Diocese of Tegucigalpa by 1916.
tehran: Tehran is bounded in the north by the southern end of the Alborz range, whose highest point near the city is Tochal Peak at 3,963 metres. The northern districts begin at about 1,800 metres, with houses and streets on steep slopes, while Rey at the southern end lies at about 1,100 metres beside the single mountain of Raga. Fertile meadows and villages, fed by the Karaj and Jajrud rivers, lie to the west and south-west. Mount Damavand, Iran's highest peak, stands near the city and figures in Ferdowsi's Šāhnāme as the homeland of Keyumars and the place where King Fereydun bound the dragon fiend Zahhak.

The origin of the name is disputed. The city's own account derives it from the Persian words for 'bottom' and 'slope', the foot of the mountain, while the linguist Zana Kamrani proposes that it means 'the warm place', in contrast to Shemiran, 'the cool place'.

Archaeological remains from the ancient city of Ray suggest that settlement in the area is more than 6,000 years old. In the Median period part of present-day Tehran was a suburb of the prominent city of Rhages, which appears in the Avesta and in Old Persian inscriptions as a province; from there Darius I sent reinforcements to his father Hystaspes in Parthia. In 641 the last Sasanian king, Yazdgerd III, issued his final appeal to the nation from Rhages before fleeing to Khorasan. Because the city resisted the Muslim invasion, the Arabs ordered it destroyed and rebuilt by the aristocrat Farrukhzad.

In the ninth century Tehran was a well-known village, though less so than the flourishing Rhages nearby. Agha Mohammad Khan of the Qajar dynasty first chose it as the capital of Iran in 1786, because of its closeness to Iran's contested territories in the Caucasus and to avoid the rival factions of earlier dynasties. Under Reza Shah the city gained Iran's first institute of higher learning, bank, railway line and museum. Large-scale construction began in the 1920s, and Tehran became a destination for mass migration from all over Iran, especially in the 20th century.

Tehran is the capital and largest city of Iran, with 8,693,706 inhabitants at the 2016 census. Persians are the majority, with Azeris the second-largest ethnic group at about 10 to 15 per cent. Its historical sites include the Golestan Palace of the Qajar dynasty, a World Heritage Site, and the Sa'dabad and Niavaran palace complexes; the Azadi Tower was built in 1971 to mark 2,500 years of the Persian Empire.
telangana: Telangana lies on the Deccan Plateau, in the central stretch of the eastern seaboard of the Indian Peninsula, and covers 112,077 square kilometres. It borders Maharashtra and Chhattisgarh to the north and Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka to the south. The Godavari and Krishna rivers drain it, along with smaller rivers such as the Bhima, the Manjira and the Musi, but most of the land is arid. The name comes from Telinga, and was used to set the predominantly Telugu region of the old Hyderabad State apart from Marathwada and Kalyana-Karnataka.

One of the earliest known political formations here was the Aśmaka Mahajanapada, which flourished roughly between 700 and 400 BCE and was the only southern kingdom among the sixteen great Mahajanapadas. Its capital, Podana, is identified by most scholars with present-day Bodhan. The region later belonged to many empires, among them the Maurya, Satavahana, Chalukya, Chola, Rashtrakuta, Delhi Sultanate, Bahmani Sultanate and Golconda Sultanate. The region experienced a golden age under the Kakatiya dynasty, which ruled most of present-day Andhra Pradesh and Telangana from 1083 to 1323; Rudrama Devi and Prataparudra II were prominent rulers. It weakened after the attack of Malik Kafur in 1309 and was dissolved when Muhammad bin Tughluq's forces defeated Prataparudra in 1323.

From the seventeenth to the nineteenth century the Mughals and the Nizams of Hyderabad ruled the region. In 1823 the Nizams ceded the Northern Circars and the Ceded Districts to British India, which left Hyderabad a landlocked princely state. When India became independent in 1947 the Nizam wished to stay independent, and the Government of India annexed Hyderabad State on 17 September 1948 in a military operation called Operation Polo. After decades of protest by the Telangana movement, the state of Telangana was created in 2014 from the Telugu regions of the former Hyderabad State.

Telangana has Hyderabad as its capital. Telugu is the primary official language and Urdu the second; about 75 per cent of people speak Telugu and 12 per cent Urdu. Before 1948 Urdu was the official language of Hyderabad State and the language of the educated elite. At the 2011 census Hindus formed 85.1 per cent of the population and Muslims 12.7 per cent. Warangal Fort, the Kakatiya capital, has the Kakatiya Kala Thoranam, which appears on the state emblem, and the Ramappa Temple is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The state is divided into 33 districts.
telescope: The word telescope was coined in 1611 by the Greek mathematician Giovanni Demisiani for one of Galileo Galilei's instruments, presented at a banquet of the Accademia dei Lincei. In the Starry Messenger Galileo had used the Latin term perspicillum. The Greek roots are tele, far, and skopein, to look or see, giving teleskopos, far-seeing. The first practical instruments were refracting telescopes with glass lenses, used both on land and for astronomy. Word of the invention spread through Europe, and Galileo heard of it before building his own version.

Originally the telescope was an optical instrument that used lenses, curved mirrors or both to observe distant objects. The word now covers a wide range of instruments that detect different regions of the electromagnetic spectrum. There are three main optical types: the refracting telescope, which forms an image with lenses; the reflecting telescope, which uses mirrors; and the catadioptric telescope, which combines mirrors with lenses. A place holding one or more telescopes or other instruments is called an observatory.

Radio telescopes are directional antennas that usually employ a large dish. By correlating the signals received by several dishes, astronomers compute high-resolution images, a technique called aperture synthesis. X-rays are harder to focus, and X-ray telescopes use ring-shaped mirrors of heavy metals that reflect the rays at a glancing angle; Hans Wolter outlined three ways of building such a telescope in 1952. Because the atmosphere is opaque to most of the spectrum, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma-ray instruments are carried on balloons or satellites.

The idea that the light-gathering element could be a mirror instead of a lens was investigated soon after the refracting telescope appeared. Parabolic mirrors promised less spherical aberration and no chromatic aberration. In 1668 Isaac Newton built the first practical reflecting telescope, of the design now called the Newtonian reflector. The achromatic lens of 1733 partly corrected the colour fringes of simple lenses and allowed shorter, more useful refractors.

Reflectors were long hampered by mirrors of speculum metal, which tarnished quickly in the 18th and early 19th centuries. Silver-coated glass mirrors, introduced in 1857, and aluminized mirrors, from 1932, eased the problem. Refractors cannot grow beyond about one metre across, so most large research telescopes built since the turn of the 20th century are reflectors. John Dobson invented the Dobsonian telescope in 1956. The first purpose-built radio telescope began operating in 1937, and infrared telescopes followed in the 1960s.
telugu-language: Telugu descends from Proto-Dravidian, which linguistic reconstruction places around the fourth millennium BCE. It belongs to the South Dravidian-II, or South-Central Dravidian, subgroup, with Gondi, Kuvi, Koya, Pengo, Konda and Manda. The philologist Mikhail S. Andronov places its separation from Proto-Dravidian at about 1000 BCE. The name is explained as a form of Tenugu, from the Proto-Dravidian word for south, meaning the people who lived to the south of the speakers of Sanskrit and Prakrit; Telugu results from an alternation of n and l.

Its history is divided into phases. Telugu words appear early in Prakrit inscriptions, and one early word, nāgabu, found at the Amaravati Stupa, is dated to about 200 BCE. The first long inscription entirely in Telugu, dated to 575 CE, is attributed to the Renati Choda king Dhanunjaya and was found in the Kadapa district. Titles of Mahendravarman I in Telugu, from about 600 CE, are inscribed in caves in Tamil Nadu. About 10,000 pre-colonial inscriptions survive in Telugu.

Telugu is a Dravidian language native to the Indian states of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, where it is the official language, and is also official in the Yanam district of Puducherry. It is spoken by about 100 million people and is the most widely spoken member of its family. Words generally end in vowels. Its grammar has suffixes only, with three noun classes, seven cases and a basic subject-object-verb order. Most of its vocabulary is inherited from Proto-Dravidian, with many borrowings from Sanskrit. There are Telangana, Rayalaseema, Coastal Andhra and North Andhra dialects, and standard Telugu is based on the speech of educated speakers of the central dialect.

Telugu has an unbroken literary tradition of over a thousand years. The Vijayanagara Empire dominated from 1336 to the late 17th century, and Telugu literature had what is considered its Golden Age in the 16th century under Krishnadevaraya. The Venetian explorer Niccolò de' Conti, visiting in the 15th century, noted that its words end in vowels, as in Italian, and called it the Italian of the East. In the precolonial era it became the language of high culture throughout South India, which Vijaya Ramaswamy compared to the dominance of French in Europe. Telugu also predominates in Carnatic music.

Persian and Arabic influence produced a distinct variant around Hyderabad, beginning with the Delhi Sultanate in the 14th century. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries English influence and the printing press, especially in the Madras Presidency, shaped writers such as Kandukuri Veeresalingam and Gurajada Apparao. The Andhra Pradesh Official Language Act of 1966 declared Telugu the official language of the state, later divided into Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.
ten-commandments: The phrase Ten Commandments comes from Exodus 34:28, Deuteronomy 4:13 and Deuteronomy 10:4, and in each case can be translated as the ten words, sayings or matters. The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, rendered it as dekalogos, which became Latin decalogus and English Decalogue.

In the biblical narrative the revelation begins in Exodus 19, when the Israelites reach Mount Sinai, also called Horeb. On the third morning there are thunders, lightnings and a thick cloud on the mountain, and in Exodus 20 God speaks the words of the covenant to all the people. Scholars have proposed three main datings: early Mosaic authorship, a pre-exilic monarchic origin, or a postexilic composition. Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman argue for the seventh century BCE, and David H. Aaron for a date after 586 BCE.

The seventeen verses of Exodus 20:1 to 17 and Deuteronomy 5:4 to 21 are divided into ten commandments in different ways, although they contain more than ten imperatives. One approach separates the prohibition of other gods from that of images, as in the Septuagint and among Eastern Orthodox and Reformed Christians following Calvin. Another joins them, as Augustine did in the 4th century, dividing the prohibition on coveting into two. The Samaritan Pentateuch adds an instruction to sacrifice to Yahweh, which Samaritans count as the tenth.

Exodus 34:28 itself names the passage of Exodus 34:11 to 27 as the Ten Commandments, and since it concerns proper worship rather than murder or theft, some scholars call it the Ritual Decalogue and the better known text the Ethical Decalogue.

In Judaism the commandments are the foundation of rabbinic law, held to state God's universal and timeless standard, unlike the rest of the 613 commandments the tradition finds in the Torah. Most Christian traditions hold that they remain valid and divinely authoritative. In the New Testament, Jesus refers to the prohibitions of murder and adultery in the Sermon on the Mount and repeats five of them in Matthew 19. In Islam the receiving of the tablets by Moses is described in Surah A'raf, and Surah An'am 6:151 to 153 is widely taken as a reinstatement of the commandments.

After the Reformation, European Protestants replaced some visual art in churches with plaques of the Ten Commandments. In England such Decalogue boards also represented the monarch's emphasis on royal law within the churches. In 1980 the United States Supreme Court ruled unconstitutional a Kentucky statute requiring a copy in every public classroom. Hundreds of monuments were placed as publicity for Cecil B. DeMille's 1956 film The Ten Commandments.
tennessee: Tennessee is a landlocked state that borders eight others: Kentucky and Virginia to the north, North Carolina to the east, Georgia, Alabama and Mississippi to the south, and Arkansas and Missouri to the west. It is divided into three Grand Divisions, East, Middle and West Tennessee. The Blue Ridge Mountains along the eastern border reach some of the highest elevations in eastern North America, the Cumberland Plateau has scenic valleys and waterfalls, and West Tennessee has level, fertile plains. The Tennessee River crosses the state twice and the Mississippi River forms its western border.

The first inhabitants were Paleo-Indians who arrived about 12,000 years ago, at the end of the Last Glacial Period. Archaeologists name the Archaic (8000–1000 BCE), Woodland (1000 BCE–1000 CE) and Mississippian (1000–1600 CE) periods. Squash, corn, gourds and sunflowers were first grown in Tennessee during the Woodland period, when the first mounds were built, and Mississippian peoples developed organised chiefdoms and built many ceremonial structures. The state's name comes most directly from the Cherokee town of Tanasi. A Spanish party under Juan Pardo met a village called Tanasqui in 1567, and Governor James Glen of South Carolina is credited with the modern spelling in the 1750s.

The Watauga Association of 1772, a frontier pact, is generally regarded as the first constitutional government west of the Appalachian Mountains. The area was first part of North Carolina and then of the Southwest Territory, and it became the 16th state on 1 June 1796. Its constitutions date from 1796, 1834 and 1870. The capital moved among Knoxville, Nashville and Murfreesboro before Nashville became the permanent capital in 1843. The nickname The Volunteer State reflects a strong tradition of military service.

Tennessee was a slave state until the Civil War and was politically divided: most of the west and middle supported the Confederacy, while the east was largely pro-Union. It was the last state to secede and the first former Confederate state readmitted to the Union. In the 20th century it moved from an agrarian society to a more diversified economy, helped by the Tennessee Valley Authority and by Oak Ridge, established in the Second World War to house the Manhattan Project's uranium enrichment facilities.

Nashville is the capital and largest city; Memphis, Knoxville, Chattanooga and Clarksville follow. The state has 95 counties and about 7.2 million people. Great Smoky Mountains National Park, the most visited national park in the United States, lies in the east. Tennessee has played a major role in the development of country, blues, rock and roll, soul and gospel music, and the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville has broadcast continuously since 1925.
texas: Texas lies in the south-central United States. The Rio Grande forms its border with the Mexican states of Chihuahua, Coahuila, Nuevo León and Tamaulipas, the Red River borders Oklahoma and Arkansas, and the Sabine River borders Louisiana. One classification divides the state, from south-east to west, into the Gulf Coastal Plains, the Interior Lowlands, the Great Plains and the Basin and Range Province of Far West Texas, which holds desert valleys and wooded mountain slopes.

The name comes from the Caddo word táy:shaʼ, meaning friend, which the Spanish applied, as Tejas or Texas, to the Caddo themselves, specifically the Hasinai Confederacy. In the 18th century Spanish rule called the area Nuevas Filipinas, or the province of the Tejas, and later the province of Texas. An alternative etymology advanced in the late 19th century connected the name with the Spanish teja, roof tile.

Before European contact Texas lay between the Southwestern and Plains cultural spheres, with the Ancestral Puebloans to the west, the Mississippian culture to the east and the civilizations of Mesoamerica to the south. The languages spoken included Caddoan, Atakapan, Athabaskan, Coahuiltecan and Uto-Aztecan, besides isolates such as Tonkawa. The agricultural, mound-building Caddo controlled much of the north-east, the Karankawa lived along the central coast, and Apache peoples lived throughout the interior. No one culture dominated the whole territory.

Spain was the first European country to claim and control Texas, followed by a brief French colonization. The territory became part of Mexico after its independence from Spain in 1821. Rising tensions between settlers and the Mexican government led to the Texas Revolution, which included the Battle of the Alamo, and to the independent Republic of Texas in 1836. In 1845 Texas joined the United States as the 28th state, which helped spark the Mexican-American War.

Texas remained a slave state until the American Civil War, in which it seceded from the Union and joined the Confederate States. After the war and the restoration of its representation in the federal government, it went through a long period of economic stagnation before substantial growth in the 20th century. The current Texas Constitution was adopted in 1876.

Austin is the state capital, and the largest metropolitan areas are the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex and Greater Houston. At the 2020 census Texas had 29,145,505 residents, the second-largest population of any state after California; it is also the second largest in area, after Alaska. Its nickname, the Lone Star State, refers to the single star on the flag of the Republic of Texas.
thailand: Thailand shares land borders with Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia and Malaysia and has coasts on the Gulf of Thailand and the Andaman Sea. It covers about 513,120 square kilometres, and the Gulf of Thailand covers 320,000 square kilometres. The north is the mountainous Thai highlands, where Doi Inthanon rises to 2,565 metres. The northeast, Isan, is the Khorat Plateau, bordered on the east by the Mekong. The centre is dominated by the flat Chao Phraya River valley, which runs into the Gulf of Thailand, and the south is the narrow Kra Isthmus widening into the Malay Peninsula.

The Chao Phraya and the Mekong are the indispensable watercourses of rural Thailand, and both are used for industrial-scale production of crops. The climate is shaped by the southwest and northeast monsoons, and most of the country has a tropical savanna climate.

Rice cultivation began around 2000 BCE, and the Ban Chiang site in the northeast is the earliest known centre of copper and bronze production in Southeast Asia, dating between 2000 and 1000 BCE. By the 6th century early multiethnic kingdoms had emerged, including the Mon principalities of Dvaravati and Hariphunchai, and in the 9th century the Khmer people established the Khmer Empire, centred in Angkor. Historians suggest the ancestors of the Thai people migrated from southern China and northern Vietnam between the 6th and 11th centuries, intermixing with Mon and Khmer populations.

King Ramkhamhaeng's reign (1279 to 1298) marked the inception of a unified Thai identity. After the destruction of Ayutthaya in 1767, King Taksin established the Thonburi Kingdom, and Rama I moved the capital to Bangkok in 1782. Siam was the only country in Southeast Asia to avoid European colonisation, though it ceded territory and trade rights through unequal treaties. The People's Party carried out a bloodless revolution on 24 June 1932, and the country was officially renamed Thailand on 24 June 1939.

Thailand has had 20 constitutions and charters since 1932, and all state that politics operate within a constitutional monarchy. The National Assembly has a 200-member Senate and a 500-member House of Representatives. The population is about 66 million, and Theravada Buddhism is central to modern Thai identity.
thales-of-miletus: Thales came from Miletus, a mercantile city at the mouth of the Maeander River in Ionia. The main source for the details of his life is the third-century CE writer Diogenes Laërtius, who wrote some eight centuries after Thales's death and drew on sources that often contained unreliable or even fabricated information. Herodotus called him a Phoenician by remote descent, and Diogenes names his parents as Examyas and Cleobulina, but other writers represent him as a genuine Milesian of distinguished family.

Later writers said that he visited Egypt, where he learned geometry, or Babylonia. Scholars dispute this, since such journeys were a commonplace attribution to philosophers by later writers explaining the origin of their mathematical knowledge.

Thales is counted among the Seven Sages of Greece, semi-traditional statesmen and founding figures, and Diogenes calls him the first of them. The Delphic maxim know thyself was attributed to him. Diogenes also tells of a gold tripod or bowl to be given to the wisest man, which passed round the sages and returned to Thales, who dedicated it to Apollo. According to Diogenes he advised the Milesians not to join the Lydians in a symmachia, a fighting together; when King Croesus was defeated by Cyrus the Great, Miletus was spared because it had taken no action.

Herodotus reported that Thales predicted a solar eclipse in 585 BCE. He also tells that Thales got the army of Croesus across the river Halys by digging a diversion upstream, though he himself finds the story doubtful.

Thales sought to explain natural phenomena by rational hypotheses that referred to natural processes, not to the will of gods and heroes. His best-known thesis, reported by Aristotle in the Metaphysics, is that the originating principle of nature, the arche, is a single material substance, water. Aristotle did not hold the view himself, though the attribution to Thales is generally accepted. Thales thought the Earth floats on water, and explained earthquakes as the Earth being rocked by waves.

Aristotle regarded him as the first natural philosopher, a view that most other writers did not adopt until eighteenth-century historians made it prominent. According to Aristotle he held that all things are full of gods, reasoning that lodestones and amber have souls because they cause movement. Thales is the namesake of Thales's theorem in geometry, and he was said to have calculated the heights of the pyramids and the distance of ships from the shore.
the-beatles: In November 1956 the 16-year-old John Lennon formed a skiffle group with friends from Quarry Bank High School for Boys in Liverpool, named the Quarrymen after the school song. Paul McCartney met Lennon on 6 July 1957 and joined shortly after, and in 1958 George Harrison, then 15, was enlisted as lead guitarist after playing Raunchy for Lennon on the upper deck of a Liverpool bus. Stuart Sutcliffe joined on bass in January 1960 and suggested the name Beatals, in tribute to Buddy Holly and the Crickets. By mid-August 1960 they were simply the Beatles.

The Beatles built their reputation playing clubs in Liverpool and in Hamburg, West Germany, from 1960. Ringo Starr officially joined in 1962. Manager Brian Epstein shaped them into a professional act, and the producer George Martin developed their recordings. After signing with EMI they had their first hit, Love Me Do, in late 1962. By early 1964 they were international stars, leading the British Invasion of the American pop market. They retired from live performance in 1966 and made more sophisticated albums, among them Revolver (1966) and Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band (1967). In 1968 they founded Apple Corps. The band broke up in 1970.

Their arrival in the United States in 1964 is credited with beginning the album era. Young adults abroad name them among the people they most associate with British culture. In 1965 Queen Elizabeth II appointed the four members Members of the Order of the British Empire, and they were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1988, their first year of eligibility.
the-communist-manifesto: In spring 1847 Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels joined the League of the Just, which became the League of Communists. At its first congress, held from 2 to 9 June, the League asked Engels to draft a statement of its programme. He wrote the Draft of a Communist Confession of Faith, a catechism of 22 questions, and in October produced the Principles of Communism, a longer one of 25 questions. Several scholars see the kernel of the Manifesto in this second text.

Marx delayed the work while lecturing on political economy and writing for the Deutsche-Brüsseler-Zeitung. In late January 1848 the League's Central Committee sent him an ultimatum demanding the manuscript by 1 February. The Manifesto was written over six to seven weeks, and only one page of draft is known to survive. Engels is credited as co-author, but the final text was penned by Marx; Engels wrote in 1883 that its basic thought belonged solely to Marx.

The Manifesto has a preamble and four sections. The preamble opens with the line about a spectre haunting Europe and urges communists to state their views openly. The first section, Bourgeois and Proletarians, sets out historical materialism: all earlier societies were marked by an exploiting minority and an exploited majority, and under capitalism the industrial working class, the proletariat, stands against the owners of the means of production, the bourgeoisie.

The authors argue that the bourgeoisie, by constantly revolutionising production, displaced feudal powers, and that in doing so it creates its own grave-diggers. In their view the proletariat will become conscious of its power and overthrow it, leading to a classless society. They also proposed ten measures for a society moving towards communism, which their 1872 preface called dated.

The pamphlet was published anonymously in late February 1848 in London, as a 23-page German text issued by the Communist Workers' Educational Association. Marx was expelled by the Belgian police on 4 March. The first English version, translated by Helen Macfarlane, appeared in November 1850 in George Julian Harney's Chartist paper The Red Republican, which also named the authors for the first time.

After years of obscurity the text revived in the early 1870s, through Marx's role in the First International, his support for the Paris Commune of 1871 and the treason trial of German Social Democratic leaders, where prosecutors read it into the record. A new German edition of 1872 first used the short title The Communist Manifesto. After the October Revolution of 1917 it became required reading for Leninist parties, and by its centenary in 1948 general publishers were printing it widely.
the-gambia: The Gambia is the smallest country on the African mainland. Its borders mirror the meandering Gambia River, which flows through the middle of the country, and Senegal surrounds it on all sides except the 80 kilometres of Atlantic coastline in the west. It is less than 50 kilometres wide at its widest point, with an area of 11,295 square kilometres. The present boundaries were defined in 1889 after an agreement between the United Kingdom and France, though fixing the final borders took nearly 15 years. The river, known locally as the River, is navigable deep into the continent.

The name derives from the Mandinka term Kambra or Kambaa, meaning the Gambia River. Portuguese explorers adopted a variation of it, which was later anglicised. In 1964 Prime Minister Dawda Jawara asked that the name keep the definite article, in part to reduce confusion with the newly independent Zambia.

Arab traders gave the first written accounts of the area in the ninth and tenth centuries. Muslim merchants and scholars established communities in West African commercial centres and carried out trans-Saharan trade, exporting gold, ivory and people taken captive in raids and sold as slaves. At the beginning of the 14th century most of the present Gambia was part of the Mali Empire. The Portuguese reached the area by sea in the mid-15th century and began to dominate overseas trade.

In 1588 António, Prior of Crato, a claimant to the Portuguese throne, sold exclusive trade rights on the river to English merchants, and in 1618 King James I granted a charter to an English company. Between 1651 and 1661 parts of the Gambia, including St. Andrew's Island and Fort Jakob, were ruled by the Duchy of Courland and Semigallia under Prince Jacob Kettler, before being ceded to England in 1664.

Britain and France struggled for supremacy on the Senegal and Gambia rivers through the 18th century. The 1783 Treaty of Versailles gave Britain the Gambia River, but France kept an enclave at Albreda until it was ceded in 1856. The British established the military post of Bathurst, now Banjul, in 1816, and the Gambia gained independence on 18 February 1965.

The Gambia is the Republic of The Gambia, a republic since 1970, and its capital is Banjul, an island city once called Bathurst. English is the sole official language, and Mandinka is spoken as a first language by 38 per cent of the population. The Mandinka are the most numerous ethnic group. The river and its slave-trade history are the setting of Alex Haley's Roots.
the-hague: The Hague, in Dutch Den Haag, short for 's-Gravenhage, is the capital of the province of South Holland. It lies on the west coast facing the North Sea, and its coastal area includes the seaside resort of Scheveningen. The name comes from the Middle Dutch word hag(h)e, meaning hedge, enclosure or hunting ground, and first appeared in 1242. The fuller 's-Gravenhage, the count's enclosure, appeared in 1347 and refers to the Count of Holland. The municipal government adopted the shorter name in 1990.

The area belonged to the Roman province of Germania Inferior. Little is known of the city's origin, since no contemporary documents describe it, but it was founded by the last counts of the House of Holland. Floris IV presumably bought a court by the present Hofvijver in 1229 but died in a tournament in 1234. His son William II lived there, and after he was elected King of the Romans in 1248 he had builders turn the court into a royal palace, later called the Binnenhof.
