The Ridderzaal, or Knights' Hall, was completed under his son Floris V and still stands. From the 13th century the counts of Holland used The Hague as their administrative centre and residence.

In 1806, when the Kingdom of Holland was a puppet state of the First French Empire, Louis Bonaparte granted the settlement city rights. After Belgium separated in 1830, Amsterdam stayed the capital while the government remained in The Hague. When government grew more prominent after 1850 the city expanded quickly, with streets built for civil servants and for Dutchmen retiring from the administration of the Netherlands East Indies.

The Hague is the seat of the Dutch government, the States General, the Supreme Court and the Council of State, while Amsterdam is the official capital. The Ridderzaal is still used for political events such as the annual speech from the throne. Most foreign embassies in the Netherlands are in the city. It is home to the International Court of Justice, the International Criminal Court and the Permanent Court of Arbitration, and the Royal Library of the Netherlands is also there.
the-internationale: The title comes from the First International, the alliance of workers that held a congress in 1864. Pottier intended his text to be sung to the tune of La Marseillaise, and it was reputedly sung to that tune at his burial in November 1887. An earlier version, written in September 1870, marked the Third Republic declared after Prussia's defeat of the Second French Empire and honoured the First International. The text that endures is the one Pottier authorised for his Chants Révolutionnaires, published by his fellow Communard Jean Allemane in April 1887.

The melody was composed in 1888 by Pierre De Geyter for the choir La Lyre des Travailleurs of the French Workers' Party in his hometown of Lille. He had been commissioned by Gustave Delory, the future mayor of Lille, who had received the text from a young socialist teacher, Charles Gros. Pottier's lyrics contain one-liners that became slogans, and others such as Ni Dieu, ni César, ni tribun, meaning neither God, nor Caesar, nor tribune, were already familiar in the workers' movement.

The Second International adopted the song as its official anthem, and it became a standard of the socialist movement from the late nineteenth century. The first English version has been attributed to Pottier himself, and the first US translation was made by Charles Hope Kerr, who heard it in Lille in 1894. By the time of the International Socialist Congress in Copenhagen in 1910 versions existed in 18 languages. Arkady Kots made the first Russian translation in 1902, and after the Bolshevik Revolution its future tenses were rewritten in the present. Qu Qiubai made a new Chinese translation in 1923, and the song was played at the close of the Chinese Communist Party's third National Congress that year.

In the Soviet Union it was the national anthem until it was replaced by the State Anthem of the USSR; Arturo Toscanini's orchestration of it was broadcast in 1943 for the anniversary of the October Revolution. In South Africa communists, unionists and activists of all races sang it until the Communist Party was suppressed from 1950.

Pierre De Geyter's authorship was obscured. To protect his job as a woodcarver, the first leaflets gave only the French form of his name, Degeyter, and a second edition named his brother Adolphe as the composer. Pierre lost a lawsuit over this in 1914 and was legally recognised as the author only in 1922. Adolphe died in 1916, leaving a note explaining the fraud. Pierre De Geyter died in 1932, and the music is now in the public domain.
theatre: Modern Western theatre comes in large measure from the theatre of ancient Greece, from which it takes technical terms, classification into genres and many themes, stock characters and plot elements. Western theatre originated in the city-state of Athens, as part of a wider culture of performance that included festivals, religious rituals, law, athletics, music and poetry. Attendance at the City Dionysia was an important part of citizenship. The Greeks also developed dramatic criticism and theatre architecture.

According to Aristotle, the first theoretician of theatre, its origins lie in festivals honouring Dionysus. Greek drama consisted of tragedy, comedy and the satyr play. Athenian tragedy emerged in the sixth century BCE and flowered in the fifth. Playwrights at the City Dionysia presented a tetralogy, usually three tragedies and one satyr play. Official records begin in 501 BCE, when the satyr play was introduced. Of more than a thousand tragedies performed in the fifth century BCE only 32 survive, with complete texts by Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides.

Theatre is a collaborative art that uses live performers, usually actors, to present a real or imagined event before a live audience in a specific place, often a stage. The word comes from the Ancient Greek théatron, a place for viewing. Greek performances took place in semi-circular auditoria cut into hillsides, seating 10,000 to 20,000 people, with a dancing floor called the orchestra and a scene building called the skene. The actors, always men, wore masks and each might play several parts. Modern musical theatre emerged from comic opera, variety, vaudeville and music hall in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

Theatre has been part of human culture for more than 2,500 years and has produced many theories. Aristotle's Poetics, from about 335 BCE, is the earliest surviving example and has influenced theories ever since. He held that tragedy has six parts, in order of importance plot, character, thought, diction, song and spectacle. Konstantin Stanislavski treated theatre as an art autonomous from literature, and his system of actor training spread across Europe and the United States.
theodore-roosevelt: Theodore Roosevelt Jr. was born at 28 East 20th Street in Manhattan on 27 October 1858, the son of the businessman Theodore Roosevelt Sr. and Martha Stewart Bulloch. A sickly child with debilitating asthma, he overcame his health problems through vigorous exercise, which he called the strenuous life. He was homeschooled, solid in geography and bright in history, biology, French and German, but weak in mathematics and the classical languages. He entered Harvard University in September 1876, and his father's sudden death in 1878 devastated him. His book The Naval War of 1812, published in 1882, remains a standard study of the war.

In 1881 Roosevelt won election to the New York State Assembly. He lost the 1886 race for mayor of New York City, finishing third, and served on the United States Civil Service Commission from 1889 to 1895, fighting the spoilsmen. Appointed Assistant Secretary of the Navy in 1897, he called for a build-up of naval strength. When the Spanish–American War began in 1898 he resigned to form the Rough Riders with Colonel Leonard Wood, and returning a war hero he won the New York governorship by just 1 per cent.

Chosen as William McKinley's running mate in 1900, he became president when McKinley, shot by the anarchist Leon Czolgosz, died on 14 September 1901. He was elected to a full term in 1904 and, keeping his pledge not to run again, secured the 1908 nomination for William Howard Taft. After failing to win the Republican nomination in 1912 he founded the Bull Moose Party, and the split let the Democrat Woodrow Wilson win. He then led an expedition to the Amazon basin, where he nearly died of tropical disease. His offer to lead volunteers to France in the First World War was rejected, and he died on 6 January 1919.

Roosevelt's Square Deal had three main goals: conservation of natural resources, control of corporations and consumer protection. In 1902 he opposed the merger that created the Northern Securities Company, challenging the banker J. P. Morgan, and he sought a larger regulatory role for the federal government in place of 19th-century laissez-faire. Henry Kissinger's analysis holds that he was the first president to hold that the United States had a duty to make its power felt globally. His Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine held that the United States had to police the Western Hemisphere, lest European powers intervene there. He also made the White House the daily centre of news, and is credited with inventing the presidential press briefing.
theory-of-relativity: Albert Einstein published special relativity in 1905, building on results of Albert A. Michelson, Hendrik Lorentz, Henri Poincaré and others, with later work by Max Planck, Hermann Minkowski and others. He developed general relativity between 1907 and 1915, with contributions from many others after 1915, and its final form was published in 1916. The name comes from the expression 'relative theory' used by Planck in 1906, who stressed how the theory uses the principle of relativity. Much of the background lay in attempts to detect the luminiferous aether, the hypothetical medium thought to carry light waves. The Michelson-Morley experiment, performed in 1881 and again in 1887, found no aether wind.

Special relativity is a theory of the structure of spacetime, introduced in Einstein's 1905 paper on the electrodynamics of moving bodies. It rests on two postulates: the laws of physics are the same for all observers in any inertial frame, and the speed of light in vacuum is the same for all observers regardless of the motion of the source. Its consequences include the relativity of simultaneity, time dilation, in which moving clocks tick more slowly, length contraction, a finite maximum speed, and the equivalence of mass and energy, E = mc2.

General relativity is a theory of gravitation. It began with the equivalence principle, under which accelerated motion and rest in a gravitational field are physically identical, so that free fall is inertial motion. Einstein proposed that spacetime is curved, and after discussion with the mathematician Marcel Grossmann he formulated the theory in Riemannian geometry. In 1915 he devised the Einstein field equations, which relate the curvature of spacetime to the mass, energy and momentum within it. Its consequences include gravitational time dilation, the precession of orbits, as observed in the orbit of Mercury, and the bending of light.

By the 1920s the physics community understood and accepted special relativity, and it became a necessary tool in atomic physics, nuclear physics and quantum mechanics. General relativity at first seemed less useful, since its assertions were mostly on an astronomical scale and its mathematics was difficult. Around 1960 it became central to physics and astronomy, as discoveries such as quasars (1963), the microwave background radiation (1965), pulsars (1967) and the first black hole candidates (1981) were explained by it. The theory superseded a 200-year-old mechanics created chiefly by Isaac Newton, and predicted neutron stars, black holes and gravitational waves.
thessaloniki: Thessaloniki stands on the Thermaic Gulf, at the northwest corner of the Aegean Sea, bounded on the west by the delta of the Axios and on the southeast by Mount Chortiatis. It lies 502 kilometres north of Athens. Under the Roman Empire the Via Egnatia carried trade between Rome and Byzantium through the city and linked the empire with Asia, notably the Silk Road.

Cassander of Macedon founded the city around 315 BCE, on or near the ancient town of Therma, and named it after his wife Thessalonike, a half-sister of Alexander the Great. Under the kingdom of Macedonia it kept its own autonomy and became the most important city in Macedonia, though Pella remained the capital. In the Byzantine Empire it was the second city after Constantinople in wealth and size, with 150,000 inhabitants in the mid-12th century, until it passed to Venetian control in 1423.

Sultan Murad II captured and sacked the city in 1430; contemporary reports estimated that about one-fifth of its population was enslaved. Under Ottoman rule it was one of the empire's most important trading hubs, and Sephardic Jews arriving from Spain made its Jewish community mostly Sephardic. The city passed to the Kingdom of Greece on 8 November 1912. In 1917 a great fire destroyed much of the centre, and planners including Thomas Mawson and Ernest Hébrard rebuilt it on a plan of axes, diagonal streets and monumental squares.

Thessaloniki is the second-largest city of Greece and the capital of the region of Central Macedonia. The municipality had 319,045 inhabitants in 2021 and the metropolitan area 1,006,112. Its Paleochristian and Byzantine monuments form a World Heritage Site, and the Ano Poli, the old town that escaped the fire, is also heritage-listed. The Roman forum, found by accident in the 1960s, is among its sites. Aristotle University, founded in 1926, is the largest university in Greece.
thimphu: Thimphu lies in the western central part of Bhutan, in the narrow, linear valley of the Wang Chhu, also called the Thimphu River, which flows out into India as the Raidāk. The city extends north and south along the west bank and stands between 2,248 and 2,648 metres above sea level, making it the highest capital in Asia. The surrounding hills range from 2,000 to 3,800 metres, and the two altitude zones, warm temperate and cold temperate, decide the vegetation of the valley. At its southern end the Lungten Zampa bridge connects the east and west banks of the river. The city has no airport of its own and relies on Paro, about 52 kilometres away by road.

Before 1960 Thimphu was a group of hamlets scattered across the valley, among them Motithang, Changangkha, Changlimithang, Langchupakha and Taba. In 1885 a battle at what is now the Changlimithang sports ground ended in a decisive victory that opened the way for Ugyen Wangchuck, the first King of Bhutan, to control virtually the whole country. Under the Wangchuck dynasty the country enjoyed peace and progress under reformist monarchs. The third king, Jigme Dorji Wangchuck, abolished serfdom, redistributed land and reformed taxation and the executive, legislative and judicial systems.

The capital was moved from the ancient capital of Punakha to Thimphu, and in 1961 Thimphu was officially declared the capital of the Kingdom of Bhutan by Jigme Dorji Wangchuck. It was then a hamlet of a few houses built around the Tashichho Dzong. It was only after roads were built in the 1960s, and the country opened to the outside world following the coronation of the fourth king, Jigme Singye Wangchuck, that the city grew rapidly. India provided financial and other assistance.

Thimphu is the capital and largest city of Bhutan and the seat of most important political institutions, including the National Assembly and the embassies. Dechencholing Palace, the official residence of the King, lies to the north of the city. Vajrayana Buddhism is the state religion, and the chief abbot, the Je Khenpo, spends six months of the year in the Tashichho Dzong in Thimphu and six months in Punakha. The Tshechu festival, held in September or October, features mask dances in the courtyards of the dzong. Other landmarks include the Memorial Chorten, Changangkha Lhakhang, founded in the 13th century, and the National Institute of Zorig Chusum, which teaches the thirteen traditional arts and crafts of Bhutan.
thirty-years-war: The Reformation had led to the Schmalkaldic War between Protestants and Catholics within the Holy Roman Empire. The Peace of Augsburg of 1555 tried to prevent a recurrence by designating states as Lutheran or Catholic according to the religion of their ruler. It was undermined by the spread of Protestantism, particularly Calvinism, into Catholic areas, and by the fragmented structure of the empire, which had some 300 imperial estates and an Imperial Diet that met rarely. In 1608 Frederick IV, Elector Palatine formed the Protestant Union, and in 1609 Maximilian of Bavaria established the rival Catholic League.

In May 1618 Protestant nobles led by Count Thurn threw two of the Catholic Ferdinand's representatives and their secretary from the windows of Prague Castle, an episode known as the Third Defenestration of Prague. All three survived. Bohemia became the first battleground, and fighting then expanded into the Palatinate, drawing in the Dutch Republic and Spain, and later Christian IV of Denmark. In 1630 Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden landed in Pomerania with nearly 18,000 troops. His line formations and light artillery defeated the army of Tilly at Breitenfeld in September 1631.

The period from 1618 to 1635 was chiefly a civil war within the empire and largely ended with the Peace of Prague. France then entered the war in alliance with Sweden, and the empire became one theatre in a wider struggle against the Habsburgs of Austria and Spain. Related conflicts included revolts in Portugal and Catalonia in 1640, backed by France. Field armies averaged 13,000 to 20,000 men, and the forces deployed by both sides in Germany peaked at 250,000 in 1632.

The Peace of Westphalia consisted of three agreements: the Peace of Münster between Spain and the Dutch Republic, signed on 30 January 1648, the Treaty of Osnabrück between the empire and Sweden, and the Treaty of Münster between the empire and France. Talks had begun in 1642, with 109 delegations attending at one time or another. The settlement confirmed Dutch independence from Spain and reconfirmed the liberties of the German states, ending Habsburg attempts to turn the empire into a centralised state.

Estimates of the dead range from 4.5 to 8 million, most of them civilians and most after Sweden entered the war in 1630; claims of 12 million are no longer considered realistic. Collapse of local government produced landless peasants and rebellions, and witch-hunts began in Franconia in 1626, with over 900 people executed in the Bishopric of Würzburg by 1631. Historians count the war part of the General Crisis of the mid-17th century, and one lesson drawn was the need for permanent state armies.
thomas-aquinas: Thomas Aquinas was most likely born around 1225 in the family castle of Roccasecca, near Aquino, then controlled by the Kingdom of Sicily. His father, Landulf VI of Aquino, was a knight in the service of Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor, and his mother was Theodora Galluccio, Countess of Teano. He was the youngest of nine children, and the family intended him to follow his uncle Sinibald into the abbacy of Monte Cassino, where he began his education at five.

In 1239 his parents enrolled him at the studium generale in Naples, where he was presumably introduced to Aristotle, Averroes and Maimonides. At nineteen he resolved to join the Dominican Order, which did not please his family: on his way to Rome his brothers seized him and brought him back to his parents.

Although he wrote actively for only about two decades, Thomas wrote over eight million words. His best-known work is the unfinished Summa Theologiae (1265 to 1274), alongside the Disputed Questions on Truth (1256 to 1259), the Summa contra Gentiles (1259 to 1265) and commentaries on Scripture and on Aristotle.

Thomas treated theology as a science whose data are Scripture and the tradition of the Church, and held that faith and reason, distinct but related, are both necessary for true knowledge of God. He held that rational thinking and the study of nature, like revelation, are valid ways to understand truths about God. His central thought was that grace does not destroy nature but perfects it. He never considered himself a philosopher, and he often cites Aristotle simply as the Philosopher.

Thomas died on 7 March 1274. Dante asserts that he died by poisoning, on the order of Charles of Anjou, but the account of one of his friends gives no hint of foul play. In 1277 Étienne Tempier, bishop of Paris, issued a condemnation listing 219 propositions, twenty of them Thomistic, which severely damaged Thomas's reputation for many years. On 18 July 1323 Pope John XXII, seated in Avignon, pronounced him a saint, and his remains were moved to the Church of the Jacobins in Toulouse on 28 January 1369.
thomas-hobbes: Thomas Hobbes was born in Westport, now part of Malmesbury in Wiltshire. He later reported that his mother, hearing of the coming invasion of the Spanish Armada, gave birth prematurely: "my mother gave birth to twins: myself and fear." His father, also Thomas, was vicar of Charlton and Westport; according to the biographer John Aubrey he was uneducated and disesteemed learning. After a fight with local clergy outside his church he was forced to leave, and the family was left in the care of his older brother Francis, a wealthy glove manufacturer. Hobbes graduated from the University of Cambridge in 1608.

Hobbes became a tutor to the Cavendish family, and in 1636 he visited Galileo Galilei in Florence, then under house arrest. He later joined the philosophical groups in Paris gathered by Marin Mersenne. Back in England in 1637, he had written The Elements of Law, Natural and Politic by the end of the Short Parliament in 1640; it circulated only in manuscript until a pirated edition about ten years later.

When the English Civil War began in August 1642 and the royalist cause declined from mid-1644, many royalists came to Paris, and their company renewed his political interests. From 1647 until 1648 he was mathematical instructor to Charles, Prince of Wales. The exiled royalists led him to write Leviathan, which compares the state to a monster composed of men, created under pressure of human needs and dissolved by civil strife arising from human passions.

In Leviathan Hobbes begins from a mechanistic understanding of human beings and asks what life would be like without government, a state of nature in which each person has a right to everything. This, he argues, would lead to a war of all against all, with life "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short." In 1658 he published De Homine, completing the system he had planned more than nineteen years before. After the Restoration, his former pupil Charles II granted him a pension of £100. Hobbes died on 4 December 1679 at Hardwick Hall, aged 91, and was interred at Ault Hucknall in Derbyshire.
thomas-jefferson: Thomas Jefferson was born on 13 April 1743 (2 April, Old Style) at the family's Shadwell Plantation in the Colony of Virginia, the third of ten children. His father, Peter Jefferson, was a planter and surveyor, and his mother was Jane Randolph. He was born into a slave-owning family and remained a slave owner all his life. He was admitted to the Virginia bar in 1767.

Between 1769 and 1775 Jefferson represented Albemarle County in the Virginia House of Burgesses. In 1769 he wrote and sponsored legislation giving masters of slaves discretion to emancipate them; it met strong opposition. Elected to the Second Continental Congress in 1775, he was named to the Committee of Five with John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Robert R. Livingston and Roger Sherman. Adams persuaded the committee to choose Jefferson to write the Declaration of Independence, which Congress passed in 1776. Jefferson drafted it largely alone.

In 1784 he joined Franklin and Adams in Paris and then succeeded Franklin as Minister to France, serving five years. President George Washington appointed him the first Secretary of State, and he clashed with Alexander Hamilton over the national debt and the site of the capital, settled by the Compromise of 1790 in favour of the Potomac River. With James Madison he founded the Democratic-Republican Party in 1792. He lost to John Adams in 1796, by 71 votes to 68, and became vice president, then won the presidency in 1800 and was sworn in on 4 March 1801.

As president he defended American shipping against the Barbary pirates and British trade policies, acquired the Louisiana Territory, which doubled the nation's size, and reduced military forces and spending. His second term brought the trial of Aaron Burr and, in 1807, the Embargo Act. In 1819 he founded the University of Virginia, designed its buildings and was its first rector from 1825.

Jefferson followed the ideals of John Locke, Francis Bacon and Isaac Newton. He regarded the independent yeoman as the ideal of republican virtue, distrusted cities and financiers, and favoured decentralised government. He wrote the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom and pressed for a wall of separation between church and state. His views became known as Jeffersonian democracy. From 1768 he built Monticello in the Palladian style, with the help of local masons and carpenters and of his slaves. Historians acknowledge his lifelong ownership of large numbers of slaves but differ on his views of slavery.
thomas-more: Thomas More was born in the City of London on 7 February 1478, the second of six children of Sir John More, a successful lawyer and later a judge, and his wife Agnes. He was educated at St. Anthony's School and from 1490 to 1492 served John Morton, Archbishop of Canterbury and Lord Chancellor, as a household page. According to his friend Desiderius Erasmus, he once seriously considered becoming a monk, and between 1503 and 1504 he lived near the Carthusian monastery outside the walls of London. He chose to remain a layman, was elected to Parliament in 1504 and married Joanna Colt the following year.

In 1504 More was elected to Parliament for Great Yarmouth, and from 1510 he represented London. Between 1512 and 1519 he worked on a History of King Richard III, which he never finished. Utopia, a frame narrative in Latin, was published by Erasmus at Leuven in 1516; More is a character in it, discussing modern ills in Antwerp with the traveller Raphael Hythlodaeus, who describes the island of Utopia. After the fall of Wolsey, More became Lord Chancellor in 1529. Heresy was the most time-consuming issue of his chancellorship. He saw the Reformation as a threat to the unity of church and society, and he denied stories of torture of Protestants in his Apologia of 1533. Modern commentators remain divided over his campaign against Protestantism.

In 1533 More refused to attend the coronation of Anne Boleyn, and he was later imprisoned in the Tower of London, where he wrote A Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation. At his trial on 1 July 1535 he argued that his silence on the new statutes could be taken as consent. He was executed on Tower Hill on 6 July 1535, declaring that he died the king's good servant, and God's first. He was beatified in 1886 and canonised in 1935, and in 1980 the Church of England added him to its calendar of Reformation martyrs.
thomas-paine: Thomas Paine was the son of Joseph Pain, a tenant farmer and stay-maker, and Frances Pain, born Cocke. His father was a Quaker and his mother an Anglican. He attended Thetford Grammar School from 1744 to 1749 and at 13 was apprenticed to his father. At 19 he served as a privateer aboard the King of Prussia, and in 1759 he became a master staymaker in Sandwich, Kent. He married Mary Lambert that year, but his business collapsed, and she and their child died in early labour at Margate. He was using the spelling Paine by 1769, while living in Lewes, Sussex.

Paine barely survived the voyage to Philadelphia, where typhoid fever killed five passengers, and in March 1775 he became editor of the Pennsylvania Magazine. Common Sense appeared on 10 January 1776, signed by an Englishman. He estimated that it sold 100,000 copies in three months, though some historians dispute such figures. Benjamin Rush suggested the title, since Paine had called it Plain Truth.

Rights of Man, a tract of some 90,000 words answering Edmund Burke, appeared on 13 March 1791. Its second part proposed state support for the poor, public education and pensions for workers from the age of 50. Agrarian Justice argued that landed property had robbed most people of a natural inheritance, and proposed a national fund paying fifteen pounds to each person at the age of twenty-one. In The Age of Reason he wrote that he believed in one God and in no church. He was also an abolitionist, and Rush later credited him with a Pennsylvania Magazine article against slavery.

Paine stayed in France until 1802 and returned to the United States at Thomas Jefferson's invitation, to find himself disliked by the devout and by the Federalists. He died on 8 June 1809 at 59 Grove Street in Greenwich Village, aged 72. The Quakers refused to bury him in their graveyard, so he was buried on his farm at New Rochelle. In 1819 William Cobbett dug up the bones to give him a reburial in England that never took place, and they were later lost. His writings gave radical societies in England and Wales in the early 1790s a boost to their confidence. A marble column raised in New Rochelle in 1839 is the oldest memorial to him.
thucydides: Little is known of Thucydides's life, and the most reliable information comes from his own History. He identifies himself as an Athenian, gives his father's name as Olorus and names his deme as Halimous. He fought in the war, survived the Plague of Athens, which killed Pericles and many other Athenians, and records that he owned gold mines at Scapte Hyle in Thrace, opposite the island of Thasos. A story that as a boy he heard Herodotus lecture and wept with joy is disputed and most likely comes from a later account.

Because of his influence in the Thracian region, Thucydides was sent as a general to Thasos in 424 BCE. In the winter of 424 to 423 BCE the Spartan general Brasidas attacked Amphipolis, half a day's sail to the west, and the Athenian commander there, Eucles, sent to Thucydides for help. Brasidas, aware of Thucydides's influence with the people of Amphipolis, offered moderate terms, and the city surrendered before Thucydides arrived. Its fall caused consternation in Athens and was blamed on him, although he claimed he had been unable to reach it in time. He was exiled.

Later sources on his life are less reliable. Pausanias says a law passed by Oenobius allowed him to return to Athens after the war ended in 404 BCE and that he was murdered on the way, while Plutarch preserves a tradition that he was murdered at Scapte Hyle and that his remains were brought to Athens. Many doubt the first account, and the evidence suggests he may have lived as late as 397 BCE or slightly later.

Thucydides began to write the History of the Peloponnesian War at the outbreak of the war in 431 BCE, believing it of unmatched importance, and intended it as a possession for all time. It breaks off in the middle of 411 BCE, after the Athenian defeat at Syracuse, so it does not cover the last seven years of the war. The division into eight books was probably made after his death by scholars of Alexandria. He values eyewitness testimony, consulted written documents and interviewed participants, and unlike Herodotus he does not acknowledge divine intervention in human affairs.

He admired Pericles and disliked the demagogues who followed him, such as Cleon and Hyperbolus, but his account is generally even-handed, and he does not minimise the effect of his own failure at Amphipolis. Scholars have seen in him the influence of the Sophists and of Hippocratic medical writing, and the Melian dialogue and his version of Pericles's Funeral Oration are widely studied. Historians such as Jacqueline de Romilly have stressed his concern with Athenian imperialism, and others have read him as a tragedian in the tradition of Homer.
thuringia: Thuringia is a landlocked state in the middle of Germany, bordered by Bavaria, Hesse, Lower Saxony, Saxony and Saxony-Anhalt. It has been called the green heart of Germany since the late 19th century because of its broad, dense forest, and most of it lies in the drainage basin of the Saale, a left-bank tributary of the Elbe. The Thuringian Basin is the driest part of Germany, with only 400 to 500 mm of rain a year. The natural vegetation is beech forest, though centuries of settlement mean that most plains are cleared for farming and most forests are planted with spruce and pine.

The name derives from the Germanic tribe of the Thuringii, who emerged during the Migration Period. Their origin is largely unknown: an older theory made them successors of the Hermunduri, which later research rejected, and other historians argue that they were allies of the Huns. They were first mentioned around 400, when they were known for their excellent horses. The first documented duke of Thuringia was a local noble, Radulf I, appointed by King Dagobert I in the early 630s. He secured the borders on the Saale against Slavic incursions, but in 641 or 642 rebelled against Dagobert's successor Sigebert III and declared himself king of Thuringia.

In the Middle Ages the Saale marked the border between Germanic and Slavic territories, and the movement of eastward settlement assimilated the Slavic population between the 11th and 13th centuries. Thuringia generally accepted the Protestant Reformation, and Roman Catholicism was suppressed as early as 1520. The German Peasants' War of 1525 destroyed many churches and monasteries, and Thomas Müntzer was active among the Anabaptists of Mühlhausen. Catholicism survived within the modern borders only in the Eichsfeld, ruled by the Archbishop of Mainz, and in and near Erfurt.

The modern state was established in 1920 under the Weimar Republic by merging the Ernestine duchies; only Saxe-Coburg voted to join Bavaria instead, and Weimar became the capital. After the Second World War Thuringia lay in the Soviet occupation zone, became part of the German Democratic Republic in 1949, and was dissolved in 1952 into the districts of Erfurt, Suhl and Gera. It was re-established in 1990 after reunification. The Free State of Thuringia has about 2.1 million inhabitants, and its capital and largest city is Erfurt. The Wartburg castle, Classical Weimar and Bauhaus Weimar are UNESCO World Heritage Site listings, and the University of Jena was founded in 1558.
tianjin: Tianjin lies on the west coast of the Bohai Gulf, surrounded by Hebei Province on every side except the sea, with Beijing about 120 kilometres to the northwest. Its main urban area stands along the Hai River, which connects to the Yellow and Yangtze rivers by the Grand Canal. The land was formed between 900 and 1300 CE by sediments from rivers entering the sea at the Bohai Gulf. The name, written 天津, means the ford of the emperor, and its origin is disputed; the most common theory holds that the Yongle Emperor of the Ming bestowed it after crossing the Gu River on his way south to overthrow his nephew, the Jianwen Emperor.

The Grand Canal, running from Hangzhou to the Beijing and Tianjin region by 609 CE, carried southern grain north and helped the area's development. Tianjin appears increasingly in records under the Song dynasty and gained importance under the Yuan as a storage place for goods and grain. Under the Ming it was a garrison town and shipping station, and the walled city was built in 1404. By the 17th century it was a centre of commerce.

In the Second Opium War the British and French captured the Taku forts near Tianjin in May 1858, and the Treaty of Tientsin signed that June opened the city to foreign trade; the Xianfeng Emperor ratified the treaties in 1860. Between 1895 and 1900 Japan, Germany, Russia and other powers joined Britain and France in establishing self-contained concessions, each with its own prisons, schools, barracks and hospitals, which left churches and thousands of villas. During the Boxer Rebellion the city was the seat of the Tianjin Provisional Government.

Tianjin fell to Japan on 30 July 1937, though the Japanese generally respected the foreign concessions until 1941. In June 1939 the Japanese army blockaded the British concession in the Tientsin Incident. In the Pingjin Campaign of the Chinese Civil War the city was taken after 29 hours of fighting, and the Chinese Communist Party held it from 15 January 1949.

Tianjin is a provincial-level municipality of China with 13,866,009 people at the 2020 census, and the largest coastal city of northern China. Its seaport remains the gateway to Beijing, and some European-style buildings of the concessions are preserved.
tibet: Tibet covers much of the Tibetan Plateau and is the homeland of the Tibetans. It is the highest region on Earth, with an average elevation of 4,380 m, and its southern edge in the Himalayas includes Mount Everest at 8,848 m. Several major rivers rise on the plateau, among them the Yangtze, the Yellow River, the Indus, the Mekong, the Ganges and the Salween. Cultural Tibet is divided into Amdo in the northeast, Kham in the southeast, and Ü-Tsang with Ngari in the centre and west.

In the 7th century the Yarlung dynasty of central Tibet expanded into neighbouring regions such as Zhangzhung and Amdo, and by the 9th century the Tibetan Empire stretched from the Tarim Basin and the Pamirs in the west to Yunnan and Bengal in the southeast. After the empire dissolved, the region divided among principalities and tribal groups. Under the Mongol Yuan dynasty the Sakya lama kept a degree of autonomy as political authority, while an appointed administrator, the dpon-chen, held administrative and military power.

Between 1346 and 1354 Tai Situ Changchub Gyaltsen overthrew the Sakya and founded the Phagmodrupa dynasty, and the disciples of Je Tsongkhapa founded the Gelug school and the monasteries of Ganden, Drepung and Sera near Lhasa. In 1578 Altan Khan of the Tümed Mongols gave the Gelug lama Sonam Gyatso the title Dalai Lama. The 5th Dalai Lama (1617–1682), helped by Güshi Khan of the Khoshut Khanate, defeated the Kagyu and Jonang sects and the Tsangpa prince, and his government, the Ganden Phodrang, ruled the heartland.

Qing rule began with an expedition in 1720 that expelled the invading Dzungars. Amdo came under Qing control in 1724 and eastern Kham was joined to neighbouring Chinese provinces in 1728. The Qing sent resident commissioners called Ambans to Lhasa, and after a riot in 1750 in which the Ambans and many Han Chinese and Manchus were killed, they restored the Dalai Lama as ruler while giving the Ambans a larger part in Tibetan affairs.

Lhasa is the traditional capital, and the Potala Palace and Norbulingka, former residences of the Dalai Lama, are World Heritage Sites there. China governs most of the historical area as the Tibet Autonomous Region and as autonomous prefectures within Gansu, Sichuan, Qinghai and Yunnan. Tibetan Buddhism is the main religion and shapes the region's art, music and festivals; Bön is the indigenous religion.
tigris: The Tigris is about 1,750 kilometres long. It rises in the Taurus Mountains of eastern Turkey and flows for 400 kilometres through south-eastern Turkey before forming part of the border between Syria and Turkey. Its tributaries include the Great and Little Zab. Near its confluence with the Euphrates it splits into several channels that feed the marshes, and the main channel joins the Euphrates near al-Qurnah to form the Shatt al-Arab.

Ancient writers such as Pliny held that the two rivers once had separate outlets to the sea. The Tigris has long been a transport route in a largely desert country: shallow-draft vessels can reach Baghdad, while rafts were needed downstream from Mosul. It has also been prone to floods after the April melting of snow in the Turkish mountains.

The name comes through Latin Tigris and Greek Tígris from Old Persian Tigrā, which came from Akkadian Idiglat and Sumerian Idigna. The Sumerian name can be read as the swift river, in contrast to the Euphrates, which flowed more slowly and deposited more silt. In ancient times many of the great cities of Mesopotamia stood on or near the Tigris and drew water from it to irrigate the civilisation of the Sumerians; the city of Lagash was irrigated from the river by a canal dug around 2900 BCE.

In Sumerian mythology the god Enki created the Tigris by filling it with flowing water. In the Book of Genesis it is the third of the four rivers branching from the river that issues out of Eden. The Mandaeans use the river for baptism, and the river appeared on the coat of arms of Iraq from 1932 to 1959.
timbuktu: Timbuktu stands on the southern edge of the Sahara, about 15 to 20 kilometres north of the main channel of the Niger. It is surrounded by sand dunes, and its streets are covered in sand. The port of Kabara lies 8 kilometres to the south. The town's wealth and very existence depended on its place as the southern end of a trans-Saharan trade route.

The one good now routinely carried across the desert is rock salt, cut in slabs at Taoudenni, 664 kilometres to the north. Until the second half of the 20th century large caravans of several thousand camels took three weeks each way. The climate is a hot desert one, with most rain between June and September.

Timbuktu began as a seasonal settlement and became permanent early in the 12th century. After the visit by Mansa Musa around 1325 it flourished on the trade in salt, gold and ivory, and Mansa Musa recruited scholars from across the Islamic world. In the first half of the 15th century the Tuareg held the city for a short period, until the Songhai Empire absorbed it in 1468. A Moroccan army defeated the Songhai in 1591 and made Timbuktu its capital; the invaders formed a ruling class, the Arma, who after 1612 were virtually independent of Morocco.

The French took over Mali in 1893, and colonial rule lasted until 1960. Leo Africanus, born in Granada in 1485 and educated in Fes, visited the city and wrote an account in Italian that gave Europeans most of what they knew of Africa for centuries.

Timbuktu is the capital of the Tombouctou Region of Mali. It has three notable mosques: Djinguereber, built in 1327 under Mansa Musa, Sankoré, built in the 14th or 15th century, and Sidi Yahya, founded in 1400 and completed in 1440. In December 1988 the World Heritage Committee inscribed parts of its historic centre. The city was a world centre of Islamic learning from the 13th to the 17th century, and hundreds of thousands of manuscripts were gathered there, hidden in cellars or buried to survive the decline; libraries in Timbuktu held up to 700,000 in 2003.
timur: Timur was born in Transoxiana near the city of Kesh, now Shahrisabz in Uzbekistan, about 80 kilometres south of Samarkand, then part of the Chagatai Khanate. He belonged to the Barlas, a Turkicized Mongol confederation. His name, Temur, means iron in Chagatai, his mother tongue. Timurid histories trace his descent in the male line from Tumbinai Khan, an ancestor of Genghis Khan, but no written evidence from his own lifetime links him directly to Genghis Khan. By about 1360 he had become a military leader whose troops were mostly Turkic tribesmen, and he campaigned in Transoxiana with the Khan of the Chagatai Khanate.

Timur reduced the Chagatai khans to figureheads and ruled in their name. Because he was not a descendant of Genghis Khan, Mongol tradition denied him the title of khan, so he used the title of amir and set up a puppet khan, Suyurghatmish. His first campaigns took Khwarazm and Urgench, and in 1383 he began his conquest of Persia. When Herat did not surrender he reduced it to rubble and massacred most of its citizens.

In 1398 Timur invaded the Indian subcontinent, where the Tughlaq dynasty's Delhi Sultanate had declined and most provincial governors had asserted their independence. He crossed the Indus on 30 September 1398 with a force of 90,000 and sacked Tulamba, massacring its inhabitants. Before the battle for Delhi on 17 December 1398 he slaughtered some 100,000 captives, fearing that they might revolt. In the following years he fought the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I and the Mamluk sultan of Egypt, Nasir-ad-Din Faraj, and had Ming envoys detained. Scholars estimate that his campaigns caused the deaths of millions.

In December 1404 Timur began a winter campaign against Ming China. He fell ill beyond the Syr Daria and died at Farab on 17 or 18 February 1405. He had outlived two chosen heirs, his son Jahangir and his grandson Muhammad Sultan, and on his deathbed named Muhammad Sultan's brother Pir Muhammad. A civil war among his descendants followed, and his youngest son Shah Rukh took the throne only in 1409.

His legacy is mixed. Central Asia flourished under him, while Baghdad, Damascus, Delhi and other cities were sacked and their people massacred. He keeps a positive image in Muslim Central Asia and is vilified in Arabia, Iraq, Persia and India. Two Zafarnamas written under Timurid patronage present him favourably, while the Arabic chronicle of Ahmad ibn Arabshah is far less so.
tin: Tin is a chemical element with the symbol Sn, from the Latin stannum, and atomic number 50. It is a soft, silvery-white, malleable metal that can be cut with little force, and a bent bar of tin makes a crackling sound known as the tin cry, caused by the twinning of its crystals. It resists corrosion from water. It does not occur as the native element but is extracted from ores, chiefly cassiterite, the only commercially important source, which is almost always associated with granite.

The word tin is shared among the Germanic languages and traces back to a reconstructed Proto-Germanic form; cognates include German Zinn, Swedish tenn and Dutch tin. The Latin name stannum or stagnum originally meant an alloy of silver and lead, and came to mean tin in the fourth century. The earlier Latin word was plumbum candidum, or white lead. The origin of stannum is unknown and may be pre-Indo-European.

Tin extraction and use can be dated to the beginnings of the Bronze Age around 3000 BCE. The earliest bronze objects had a tin or arsenic content of under 2 per cent and are believed to be the result of unintentional alloying. Adding a second metal to copper increases its hardness, lowers its melting temperature and gives a more fluid melt, which allowed the more complex shapes cast in closed moulds of the Bronze Age.

Arsenical bronze appears first in the Near East, where arsenic is commonly found with copper ore, but its health risks were quickly realised, and the quest for sources of the much less hazardous tin began early in the Bronze Age. This created a demand for rare tin and a trade network linking distant sources of tin to the markets of Bronze Age cultures. The first tin alloy used on a large scale was bronze, of one eighth tin and seven eighths copper; after 600 BCE pure metallic tin was produced. Pewter, an alloy of 85 to 90 per cent tin, has been used for flatware since the Bronze Age.
tirana: Tirana lies on the Plain of Tirana in the centre of Albania, between Mount Dajti to the east, hills to the south and a valley to the north that overlooks the Adriatic Sea. Its average altitude is about 110 metres. The Tiranë and Lanë rivers flow through the city. Dajti National Park lies on the mountain above it, with forests of pine, oak and beech, and the city's mountains are a popular retreat in winter, when snow often covers them although the city itself rarely receives it.

The area has been inhabited since prehistoric times, with the earliest recognised reference at the Cave of Pëllumbas, of the Palaeolithic period. Illyrians were its first population and most likely formed the core of the Illyrian kingdom of the Taulantii. After the Illyrian Wars the Romans integrated the area into their empire. The oldest surviving find from that period is a Roman house of the 3rd century, later turned into a church with a mosaic floor. A castle, possibly known as Tirkan, was built by the Byzantine Emperor Justinian I and was restored by Ahmed Pasha Toptani in the 18th century.

Tirana appears in Venetian documents of the 1350s and in 1418. The first Ottoman land registrations of 1431–32 record 60 inhabited areas with nearly 2,028 houses and 7,300 inhabitants. In 1510 Marin Barleti, in his biography of Skanderbeg, called it a small village, distinguishing Little Tirana from Great Tirana. The town was founded in 1614 by the Ottoman Albanian nobleman Sylejman Pasha Bargjini, who built the Old Mosque, a small commercial centre and a hammam. Some sources describe a bazaar with watermills already existing before 1614. In the 16th century craftsmen made silk and cotton fabrics, leather, ceramics and metal artefacts. The Et'hem Bey Mosque was completed in 1821.

The city was fairly unimportant until the 20th century, when the Congress of Lushnjë proclaimed it the capital of Albania following the Albanian Declaration of Independence of 1912. Its present appearance was shaped by two totalitarian regimes: Mussolini's, whose architects Florestano Di Fausto and Armando Brasini designed the ministry buildings, and Enver Hoxha's afterwards. The population tenfolded between 1820 and 1955, and it grew faster after the fall of communism.

Tirana is the capital and largest city of Albania and seat of its government, parliament and highest courts. The centre from the University of Tirana's Mother Teresa Square to Skanderbeg Square was declared a protected cultural area in 2000. The 2023 census counted 598,176 residents in the municipality. The airport is named after Mother Teresa.
togo: Togo is a small tropical country of 56,785 square kilometres, less than 115 kilometres wide between Ghana and Benin. It extends north from the Gulf of Guinea, where its coast is 56 kilometres long and consists of lagoons with sandy beaches, to the border with Burkina Faso. The south has a savannah and woodland plateau reaching a coastal plain with lagoons and marshes, the centre is hilly, and the north is rolling savannah. The highest mountain is Mont Agou at 986 metres, and the longest river is the Mono, at 400 kilometres.

The name Togo means 'by the water' or 'behind the sea', from the Ewe words to, 'water', and go, 'shore'. It originally referred only to the town of Togo, now Togoville, and the Germans later extended it to the whole country.

Archaeological finds indicate that societies in the area could produce pottery and process iron. Between the 11th and 16th centuries the Ewe entered the area from the west, and the Mina and Gun from the east, and most settled on the coast. The Atlantic slave trade began in the 16th century. For the next two hundred years the coastal region was a trading centre for Europeans in search of slaves, which earned Togo and the surrounding region the name the Slave Coast.

In 1884 a paper was forcibly signed at Togoville with King Mlapa III, whereby Germany claimed a protectorate over a stretch of coast and gradually extended its control inland. In 1905 this became the German colony of Togoland. The local population was forced to work, to cultivate cotton, coffee and cocoa, and to pay taxes, and a railway and the port of Lomé were built for export.

Britain and France invaded in August 1914, and German forces surrendered on 26 August. The territory was partitioned into British and French zones, which on 20 July 1922 became League of Nations mandates. French Togoland became an autonomous republic in 1956, and British Togoland voted to join the Gold Coast, as part of Ghana, in 1957. Togo became independent from France in 1960.

Togo is the Togolese Republic, with its capital, Lomé, on the Gulf of Guinea. French is the official language, and Kabiye and Ewe are national languages. The population is about 8 million, with some 40 ethnic groups, of which the Ewe in the south are the most numerous. Culture draws on Ewe and Mina traditions in the south, including the creator god Mawu and the vodun, and on Kabye and Tem traditions in the north, including the Evala wrestling initiation rite.
tokelau: Tokelau consists of three tropical coral atolls, Atafu, Nukunonu and Fakaofo, with a combined land area of about 10 square kilometres, between latitudes 8 and 10 degrees south, about midway between Hawaii and New Zealand and some 500 kilometres north of Samoa. The highest point is just 5 metres above sea level, and the islands lie in the Pacific tropical cyclone belt. Swains Island (Olohega), culturally and geographically part of the same archipelago, has been under United States control since about 1900 and is administered as part of American Samoa. The name is a Tokelauan word meaning north wind; European explorers called the group the Union Islands, and it was shortened to Tokelau on 9 December 1976.

Archaeological evidence indicates that the atolls were settled about 1,000 years ago from Samoa. The three atolls functioned separately in politics while keeping social and linguistic cohesion, governed by chiefly clans, with occasional wars between atolls as well as intermarriage; Fakaofo held some dominion over Atafu and Nukunonu. Life was subsistence-based, relying mainly on fish and coconut.

Commodore John Byron sighted Atafu on 24 June 1765, and Captain Edward Edwards visited it in June 1791 in search of the Bounty mutineers. In 1877 an Order in Council placed the islands under United Kingdom protection, and in June 1889 Commander C. F. Oldham of HMS Egeria raised the Union Flag on each atoll. They were annexed on 29 February 1916 and included in the Gilbert Islands. They were placed under the Governor-General of New Zealand in 1925, and New Zealand took over administration on 11 February 1926, though sovereignty remained with the United Kingdom.

Tokelau is a dependent territory of New Zealand, whose King is its head of state, and both governments call it a nation. About 2,500 people live there, and some 94 per cent speak Tokelauan as their first language. Since 1993 the territory has elected its own head of government, the Ulu-o-Tokelau, a post that rotates among the faipule of the three atolls, and the basis of its system is the Tokelau Islands Act 1948. Tokelauans have twice narrowly failed to reach the two-thirds majority needed for further self-determination.
toronto: Toronto stands on a harbour on the north-western shore of Lake Ontario, on a broad sloping plateau interspersed with rivers, deep ravines and urban forest. The city covers 631 square kilometres and has a 46-kilometre waterfront. The Toronto Islands and Port Lands extend into the lake and shelter the harbour south of downtown. The name was recorded in many spellings. The early form Taronto referred to the Narrows between Lake Simcoe and Lake Couchiching, which the Mohawk called tkaronto, meaning where there are trees standing in the water, a name recorded as early as 1615 by Samuel de Champlain.

Indigenous peoples have inhabited the area for more than 10,000 years. The Wendat, an Iroquoian-speaking agricultural people, farmed it for centuries before European contact, until the Haudenosaunee invaded and massacred them between 1648 and 1650. By the 1660s the Haudenosaunee had two villages in what is now Toronto, Ganatsekwyagon on the Rouge River and Teiaiagon on the Humber River. By 1701 the Mississaugas, an Anishinaabe-speaking people from northern Ontario, had displaced them at the end of the Beaver Wars. A portage route from Lake Ontario to Lake Huron, the Toronto Carrying-Place Trail, led to the wide use of the name.

French traders founded Fort Rouillé in 1750 but abandoned it in 1759 during the Seven Years' War. The British defeated the French and their Indigenous allies, and in 1763 the area became part of the colony of Quebec. After the broadly disputed Toronto Purchase, in which the Mississaugas surrendered the area to the British Crown, the British established the town of York in 1793 and later made it the capital of Upper Canada.

During the War of 1812 York was the site of the Battle of York, which caused heavy damage and a two-week occupation by American troops. It was renamed and incorporated as the City of Toronto in 1834. In 1867, at Canadian Confederation, it became the capital of the province of Ontario. The city grew beyond its original limits by annexation and amalgamation, reaching its present area in 1998. The completion of the St. Lawrence Seaway in 1959 gave ships access to the Great Lakes from the Atlantic.

Toronto is the capital of Ontario and the most populous city in Canada, with 2,794,356 people at the 2021 census. About half of its residents were born outside Canada, over 200 ethnic origins are represented, and more than 160 languages are spoken. It is governed by a mayor and a unicameral city council of 25 councillors. It is Canada's largest financial centre and the home of the Toronto Stock Exchange, and of institutions such as the National Ballet of Canada, the Canadian Opera Company and the Toronto Symphony Orchestra.
toulouse: Toulouse lies on the banks of the Garonne, 150 kilometres from the Mediterranean Sea, 230 kilometres from the Atlantic Ocean and 680 kilometres from Paris, on the axis of communication between the two seas. The Garonne valley has been a central point for trade between the Pyrenees, the Mediterranean and the Atlantic since at least the Iron Age. The historical name of the city, Tolosa, and that of its inhabitants, the Tolosates, first recorded in the 2nd century BCE, is of unknown meaning or origin, and has been connected with the Gaulish Volcae Tectosages and, by others, with a root meaning little hill.

Charlemagne created the county of Toulouse in 778 to guard the border of Muslim Spain. The disintegration of the kingdom of Aquitaine and the weakness of royal power in the following centuries led to the de facto independence of the county. The treaty of 1229 made Toulouse subordinate to the kingdom of France, and when Joan of Toulouse and her husband Alphonse of Poitiers died without heirs in 1271 the city had no count and was annexed to the royal domain. Royal officers settled in the city, trade and crafts grew, and in 1298 King Philip the Fair eased the ennobling of the capitouls, whose annually renewed council was increasingly made up of rich merchants.

The University of Toulouse was founded in 1229. In the 16th century the woad trade brought merchants of international stature to the city, and the Parlement of Toulouse made it the judicial capital of much of the south of France.

On 10 April 1814 Wellington's Hispanic-British troops fought the French under Marshal Soult at the Battle of Toulouse, four days after Napoleon's surrender, though neither army yet knew of it; it was the last Franco-British battle on French territory. In the First World War the city, sheltered from attack, gained chemical industries and aviation workshops, which began its aeronautical tradition and gave rise to the airmail company Aéropostale.

Toulouse is the prefecture of the Haute-Garonne department and of the Occitania region, with 514,819 inhabitants within its municipal boundaries in 2023. Its architecture of pinkish terracotta brick has earned it the name La Ville rose. The Basilica of Saint-Sernin, the largest remaining Romanesque building in Europe, and the former hospital Hôtel-Dieu Saint-Jacques are World Heritage Sites for their place on the pilgrimage route to Santiago de Compostela, as is the Canal du Midi, which begins in the city. Toulouse is the centre of the European aerospace industry, with the headquarters of Airbus, and its rugby club, Stade Toulousain, is among the most successful in Europe.
tractor: The word tractor comes from the Latin trahere, to pull, and the earliest recorded use for an engine or vehicle that pulls wagons or ploughs dates from 1896, from the earlier term traction motor of 1859. The first powered farm machines of the early 19th century were portable steam engines on wheels that drove other machinery through a flexible belt. Richard Trevithick designed a semi-portable barn engine in 1812 to drive a corn threshing machine, and William Tuxford of Boston, Lincolnshire, invented a truly portable engine in 1839.

The first gasoline tractors were built in Illinois by John Charter in 1889, combining single-cylinder Otto engines with a Rumely steam engine chassis. John Froelich built another in Clayton County, Iowa, in 1892 and started the Waterloo Gasoline Engine Company, but the venture failed and he was out of business by 1895.

A tractor is designed to deliver high tractive effort at slow speeds, for hauling a trailer or machinery. The earliest, called standard tractors, were meant almost only for ploughing and harrowing, which were difficult tasks for people and draft animals. Implements were first attached by a drawbar, a steel bar to which the implement's hitch was pinned, so the tractor could be used for other tasks daily. Harry Ferguson later developed the three-point hitch, which lets hydraulics raise and lower the equipment. From the 1910s to the 1950s farm mechanics in the United States often converted automobiles, especially Ford Model Ts, into tractors, and dozens of firms sold conversion kits.

Economic historians have called the farm tractor one of the most revolutionary technological innovations in the history of modern agriculture, which vastly increased farm power, raised productivity and reshaped the rural landscape. Adoption met resistance. There were 500 gas tractors in the United States in 1910 and nearly 5,000 in 1920, when 3.6 per cent of American farms had one. The share reached 13.5 per cent by the end of the 1920s and rose to 40 per cent during the Great Depression. By 1935 nearly a million tractors were in use in the United States, against 15,000 in Germany. In the 1910s and 1920s the Nebraska tests, run by the University of Nebraska, helped farmers see through marketing claims.
treaty-of-ghilajharighat: The Treaty of Asurar Ali of 1639 fixed the limit between Ahom and Mughal interests at the Barnadi river on the north bank of the Brahmaputra and the Asurar Ali on the south. During the Mughal war of succession of 1658–1659 Pran Narayan, king of Koch Bihar, attacked the Mughal faujdar at Guwahati. The Ahoms refused a Koch offer to partition Kamrup, drove the Koches out and took the whole valley up to the Sankosh River.

Aurangzeb made Mir Jumla II subahdar of Bengal. He annexed Koch Bihar in December 1661, recovered Guwahati on 5 February 1662 and occupied Garhgaon on 17 March. The rains from April turned the country to marsh and brought food shortage and cholera to the camps, while the Ahoms waged the guerrilla warfare devised by Atan Burhagohain. When the rains ended the Mughals recovered and the king withdrew to Namrup. The Ahom commander-in-chief, Baduli Phukan, defected at the end of November, and Mir Jumla, by then ill, reached Tipam by 18 December with a worn-out army eager to go home.

Atan Burhagohain persuaded the king that further fighting was futile and sent four emissaries offering tribute if the Mughals left Assam. Mir Jumla, who had refused everything short of unconditional surrender, took the opening and left the bargaining to Dilir Khan. The terms are pieced together from Persian and Assamese sources that do not fully agree.

The king accepted Mughal vassalage; his daughter Ramani Gabharu went to the imperial harem with a dowry of 20,000 tolas of gold and 120,000 of silver. The indemnity was 300,000 tolas of silver within a year and 90 elephants in instalments, the annual tribute 20 elephants. Four sons of leading nobles were to be hostages. The ceded land ran from Guwahati to the Bharali River on the north bank and to the Kolong River on the south.

The princess left on 5 January 1663 with the gold, silver and part of the elephants, and Mir Jumla ordered the retreat from Tipam on 10 January. He died on board on 31 March 1663. Jayadhwaj Singha founded a new capital at Bakata and died in November 1663; his cousin succeeded as Chakradhar Singha. Neither king could accept tributary status, and the terms were only partly fulfilled. The treaty was the root of the later conflicts, which ended with the Mughal defeat at the Battle of Saraighat in 1671 and, after the Battle of Itakhuli in 1682, the end of Mughal interests in the Brahmaputra valley.
treaty-of-versailles: The armistice of 11 November 1918 ended the fighting but left the peace to be settled. It took six months of Allied negotiations at the Paris Peace Conference to conclude a treaty. Talks between the Allies began on 18 January 1919 at the French Foreign Ministry on the Quai d'Orsay, with 70 delegates from 27 nations.

The victors wanted different things. France had lost 1.3 million soldiers and had its industrial north-east devastated, and Clemenceau sought security by weakening Germany. British opinion favoured a just peace in which Germany paid reparations. President Woodrow Wilson, whose Fourteen Points of 8 January 1918 had called for a League of Nations and self-determination, hoped for a peace of reconciliation. The result was a compromise that satisfied none of them.

The treaty was signed on 28 June 1919 in the Palace of Versailles, five years to the day after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand. Germany lost 65,000 km2 of territory and 7 million people. Alsace-Lorraine returned to France, the Saar coalfield passed to France with the territory under League of Nations control for 15 years, and Eupen-Malmedy went to Belgium. Germany's colonies became League of Nations mandates, and its concessions in Shandong were given to Japan.

The army was limited to 100,000 men, conscription was abolished and the General Staff was dissolved. Allied troops were to occupy the Rhineland for up to fifteen years. Article 231, the so-called War Guilt clause, made Germany accept responsibility for the loss and damage of the war, and a Reparation Commission was to fix the sum. The Covenant of the League of Nations formed Part I of the treaty.

Germany protested that it was excluded from the talks. The government of Philipp Scheidemann resigned rather than sign, and Gustav Bauer's government signed after an Allied ultimatum threatening an invasion across the Rhine. The United States Senate never ratified the treaty, and the United States made a separate peace with Germany.

In 1921 the Reparation Commission set Germany's share at 50 billion gold marks, later reduced by the Dawes Plan and the Young Plan. The last Allied troops left the Rhineland on 30 June 1930. Critics such as John Maynard Keynes thought the treaty too harsh, while Marshal Ferdinand Foch thought it too lenient, and historians still disagree about its effects. Resentment of the treaty, together with the stab-in-the-back myth, was exploited by Adolf Hitler, and the treaty has been cited as a cause of the Second World War.
trier: Trier lies in a hollow midway along the Moselle valley, between low vine-covered hills in the west of Rhineland-Palatinate, near the border with Luxembourg, which is some 15 kilometres away. Most of the city is on the east bank of the river. Wooded and vineyard-covered slopes stretch up to the Hunsrück plateau in the south and the Eifel in the north. The city lies within the Moselle wine region.

The Celtic tribe of the Treveri settled the area in the last pre-Christian centuries. The Romans subdued them in the 1st century BCE and founded Augusta Treverorum around 16 BCE. From 293 to 395 the city was one of the residences of the Western Roman emperor, and in the 4th century it was one of the largest cities of the empire, with some 75,000 people and perhaps as many as 100,000. The Porta Nigra dates from this age. Emperor Constantine the Great exiled Athanasius of Alexandria to Trier in 336, and Saint Ambrose was born there. The Franks seized the city in 459.

In 870 Trier became part of Eastern Francia, which developed into the Holy Roman Empire. Relics of Saint Matthias began widespread pilgrimages, and the archbishops grew powerful. The University of Trier was founded in 1473. The Trier witch trials of 1581 to 1593 reached the city itself in 1587 and led to the deaths of about 368 people. France annexed Trier in 1794 and dissolved the electoral archbishopric, and after 1815 it passed to Prussia. Karl Marx was born there in 1818.

Trier is a city of about 110,000 on the Moselle, and several Roman and medieval monuments are a World Heritage Site. They include the Porta Nigra, the best-preserved Roman city gate north of the Alps, the Aula Palatina, the throne hall of Constantine, now a Protestant church, a Roman bridge of the 2nd century still used by traffic, and the largest Roman baths north of the Alps. Trier Cathedral houses the Holy Tunic, one of a number of garments claimed to be the robe Jesus wore when he died.
trieste: Trieste lies at the head of the Gulf of Trieste, on a narrow strip of Italian territory between the sea and Slovenia, which is about 8 km to the east. Most of the city is built on a hillside at the foot of an escarpment that drops from the Karst Plateau towards the sea. The city lies where the Italian region, the Balkan Peninsula and central Europe meet. Its deep-water port is a maritime gateway for northern Italy, Germany, Austria and Central Europe.

The site has been inhabited since the second millennium BCE. The Veneti seem to have given the town its name, Tergeste, from a word for market. It became part of the Roman Republic in 177 BCE during the Second Istrian War. It belonged to the Habsburg monarchy from 1382 until 1918. Venice occupied it in 1508, but the Habsburg Empire recovered it a little over a year later. In 1719 Emperor Charles VI made it a free port, and the reign of Maria Theresa began a very prosperous era.

French troops occupied Trieste in 1797, 1805 and 1809, and from 1809 to 1813 it was part of the Illyrian Provinces, which interrupted its free port status and its autonomy. In the 19th century it was the most important seaport of the Habsburg monarchy and the fourth largest city of Austria-Hungary. James Joyce lived there between 1904 and 1915, working on Dubliners and Ulysses. Italy annexed Trieste at the end of the First World War. In 1947 it was declared the Free Territory of Trieste under United Nations protection, divided into Zones A and B along the Morgan Line; the Free Territory lasted until 1954.

Trieste is the capital and largest city of the autonomous region of Friuli-Venezia Giulia. Half the city was built in the Austro-Hungarian period, giving it some of the architecture of Vienna. Its sights include Miramare Castle, built between 1856 and 1860 for Archduke Maximilian, the Roman theatre, and the cathedral of St Justus. Piazza Unità d'Italia is the largest seafront square in Europe.
trigonometry: The word comes from the Ancient Greek trigonon, "triangle", and metron, "measure". Sumerian astronomers studied angle measure, dividing the circle into 360 degrees. They and the later Babylonians studied the ratios of the sides of similar triangles and found some of their properties, but did not make a systematic method for finding the sides and angles of triangles. The ancient Nubians used a similar method. In the 3rd century BCE Hellenistic mathematicians such as Euclid and Archimedes studied chords and inscribed angles in circles and proved theorems equivalent to modern trigonometric formulae, though they presented them geometrically rather than algebraically.

Hipparchus of Nicaea gave the first tables of chords in 140 BCE, and in the 2nd century CE Ptolemy constructed detailed tables in Book 1 of his Almagest. Ptolemy's treatise stayed in use for calculations in astronomy for the next 1,200 years in the Byzantine, Islamic and later Western European worlds.

Trigonometry relates the angles of a right triangle to the ratios of its side lengths. The sine is the ratio of the side opposite the angle to the hypotenuse, the cosine the ratio of the adjacent side to the hypotenuse, and the tangent the ratio of the opposite to the adjacent side. Their reciprocals are the cosecant, secant and cotangent. With the laws of sines and cosines one can find the remaining sides and angles of any triangle once enough of them are known. Spherical trigonometry applies the same ideas to triangles on a sphere, and was long used to locate the sun, moon and stars and to predict eclipses.

The modern definition of the sine is first attested in the Surya Siddhanta, and Aryabhata documented its properties in the 5th century CE. Medieval Islamic mathematicians translated and expanded Greek and Indian works. Habash al-Hasib al-Marwazi made the first table of cotangents in 830 CE, and by the 10th century Abu al-Wafa al-Buzjani used all six functions, with sine tables in steps of a quarter of a degree.

Nasir al-Din al-Tusi was the first to treat trigonometry as a discipline independent of astronomy, and in the 14th century Madhava of Sangamagrama developed infinite series for sine, cosine and arctangent. Knowledge reached Western Europe through Latin translations of the Almagest and the works of al-Battani and al-Tusi. Regiomontanus wrote De Triangulis in the 15th century, and Copernicus devoted two chapters of De revolutionibus orbium coelestium to the basics. Bartholomaeus Pitiscus first used the word trigonometry in his Trigonometria of 1595, and Gemma Frisius described the method of triangulation still used in surveying.
tripura: Tripura is a landlocked state of about 10,491 square kilometres, bordered by Assam and Mizoram and by Bangladesh, and one of the Seven Sister States of North East India. Five ranges of hills, Baramura, Atharamura, Longtharai, Shakhan and the Jampui Hills, run from north to south with valleys between them, while Agartala stands on a plain in the west. The highest point is Betling Shib, at 939 metres. The climate is tropical savanna, with heavy monsoon rain from May to September, and more than half of the land is forest.

The Mahabharata, the Puranas and the Edicts of Ashoka are said to mention Tripura, and the Mahabharata names the region Kirat Desh, though it is unclear whether that land matched the modern state. The Twipra Kingdom ruled the area for centuries, but when its dynasty began is not documented. The Rajmala, a chronicle first written in the 15th century, lists 179 kings down to Krishna Kishore Manikya, who reigned from 1830 to 1850, but it is not a reliable source. The name is linked to the goddess Tripura Sundari, whose temple at Udaipur is one of the 51 Shakta pithas.

After 1947 Tippera district in the plains became part of East Pakistan, while Hill Tippera stayed under a regency council until 1949. On 9 September 1949 the Maharani Regent signed the Tripura Merger Agreement, making Tripura a Part C state of India. Partition cut it off: the road distance from Kolkata to Agartala grew from under 350 kilometres to 1,700. In 1947–51 an estimated 610,000 Bengali refugees entered, a number almost equal to the state's whole population, and about 1.038 million more came during the war of 1971.

Agartala is the capital and largest city. The official languages are Bengali, Kokborok and English. The 2011 census counted 3,671,032 people, and in 2001 Bengalis were almost 65 per cent of them, with 19 scheduled tribes, of which the Kokborok-speaking Tripuris are the largest. Most of the land belongs to the Tripura Tribal Areas Autonomous District Council. The sculptures at Unakoti, Pilak and Devtamura show a fusion of organised and indigenous religious art.
trondheim: Trondheim lies on the south shore of Trondheim Fjord, at the mouth of the river Nidelva, with an excellent and sheltered harbour. In the Middle Ages the river was deep enough for most boats, but in the mid-17th century an avalanche of mud and stones made it less navigable and partly ruined the harbour. Despite its northerly latitude it has a mild climate. Around the summer solstice the nights are light enough that no outdoor lighting is needed between 23 May and 19 July, while at the winter solstice the sun stands only slightly more than 3 degrees above the horizon at midday.

The settlement was founded in 997 as a trading post by the Viking king Olav Tryggvason, who named it Kaupangen, meaning market place. Shortly afterwards it came to be called Nidaros, the outlet of the river Nid. The district around it, Trondheim, meant the home of the Trønder people, and Trøndelag the law area of the Trønder. The city served as the king's seat and was the capital of Norway until 1217. From 1152 to 1537 it was the seat of the Catholic Archdiocese of Nidaros; it then became, and has remained, the seat of the Lutheran Diocese of Nidaros.

Nidaros Cathedral, begun in 1070, is the most important Gothic monument in Norway and was Northern Europe's most important Christian pilgrimage site in the Middle Ages, with routes leading to it from Oslo and from the Jämtland and Värmland regions of Sweden. Sverre Sigurdsson built the fortification Sverresborg in 1182 and 1183; it was burned in 1188 and had been restored by 1197. Kristiansten Fortress, built from 1681 to 1684, repelled invading Swedes in 1718 and was decommissioned in 1816. During the German occupation of Norway in the Second World War the city held a submarine base for the 13th U-boat Flotilla, and Vollan District Jail was used for prisoners of war and political prisoners.

Trondheim is a city and municipality in Trøndelag county, the third most populous municipality in Norway. It was incorporated as a city on 1 January 1838, and its present municipality was formed in 1964 by merger with four neighbouring municipalities, and enlarged again in 2020. The Norwegian University of Science and Technology and the research foundation SINTEF have their headquarters there, and the cathedral stands beside the Archbishop's Palace in the city centre.
tukoji-rao-holkar-iii: Tukoji was born on 26 November 1890, the son of Shivajirao Holkar, Maharaja of Indore, and Maharani Sita Bai. His father abdicated on 31 January 1903, and as the new maharaja was only thirteen a council of regency governed until he came of age. He was educated at the Daly College in Indore and at Dehradun. On 6 November 1911 he was invested with ruling powers, and in the same year he attended the coronation of King George V in London.

As ruler he founded two orders, the Order of Merit of Holkar in February 1914 and the Order of Ahilyabai Holkar on 22 November 1920. In the New Year Honours of 1918 he was made a Knight Grand Commander of the Order of the Star of India.

In January 1925 Mumtaz Begum, a courtesan and one of his mistresses, left his harem after what she described as repressive conditions and the death of her daughter, which she blamed on palace nurses. While performing in Bombay she met Abdul Bawla, a 25-year-old Memon businessman, who was threatened several times and told to send her back, and refused. On 12 January a group of assassins attacked the couple at Malabar Hill. Bawla was shot in the head and killed; Mumtaz Begum survived with a wound to the face after British officers who were nearby intervened.

She testified against nine accused, among them men of the maharaja's household. The court sentenced three men to death and three to life imprisonment. One of the latter, General Anandrao Gangram Phanse of the Indore army, escaped the death penalty after being represented by Muhammad Ali Jinnah. The court did not formally hold Tukoji responsible, but under British pressure he abdicated on 26 February 1926 and left Indore.

After his abdication he lived mainly in France. He had married three times. His senior wife, Chandravati Gawade, whom he married on 16 March 1895 when both were small children, stayed in Indore and brought up their son, the new maharaja. His second wife, Indira Talcherkar, married in 1913, also remained there and became a patron of historical research bodies such as the Rajwade Historical Research Institute.

In 1928 he married Nancy Anne Miller, who before the wedding embraced Hinduism, was received into the Dhangar community and took the name Sharmista Devi Holkar; they had four daughters.
