The Bawla case inspired a film of 1925, Kulin Kanta, and two books. Tukoji died in Paris on 21 May 1978, leaving one son and six daughters.
tunisia: Tunisia lies on the Mediterranean coast of north-west Africa, bordered by Algeria to the west and south-west and Libya to the south-east. It covers 163,610 square kilometres and has a coastline of about 1,300 kilometres. The Dorsal, the eastern extension of the Atlas Mountains, crosses the country north-eastward; north of it lies the Tell, a region of low hills and plains. The Sahel, a coastal plain on the east, is among the world's premier areas of olive cultivation, and much of the south is semi-arid and desert. Tunis, the capital, stands on a hill slope above the lake of Tunis.

Tunisia was inhabited by Berber tribes at the beginning of recorded history. Phoenicians began settling the coast from as early as the 12th century BCE, at Bizerte and Utica. Carthage, founded in the 9th century BCE, became the dominant power in the western Mediterranean after wars with the Greek city-states of Sicily. According to the Greek writer Timaeus of Tauromenium, Dido of Tyre founded it in 814 BCE, though this is regarded as legend. Its people worshipped Baal and Tanit. After the Second Punic War, in which Hannibal invaded Italy, Carthage was a client state of Rome until it was conquered in 146 BCE and made the province of Africa.

Arab Muslims conquered Tunisia in the 7th century CE, and the migration of the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym tribes in the 11th and 12th centuries accelerated the process, and by about the 15th century the region was almost completely Arabised. The Ottoman Empire took control in 1546 and held it until the French conquest of 1881. Tunisia became independent as the Tunisian Republic in 1956.

The Tunisian Revolution of 2011 overthrew President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali after 24 years in power and set off the wider Arab Spring. A new constitution was adopted on 26 January 2014, and a constitutional referendum in 2022 made it a unitary presidential republic.

The population is 12.1 million, the vast majority Arab and Muslim. Arabic is the official language, and French serves as an administrative and educational language without official status. The European Union is the first trading partner: Tunisia signed an Association Agreement with it in July 1995, the first Mediterranean country to do so.
turin: Turin lies in north-western Italy, mainly on the western bank of the River Po, surrounded on the west and north by the Alps and on the east by a high hill that continues the hills of Monferrato. Four major rivers pass through it: the Po and its tributaries the Dora Riparia, the Stura di Lanzo and the Sangone.

The Taurini, a Celto-Ligurian Alpine people, occupied the upper valley of the Po. In 218 BCE Hannibal, allied with their enemies the Insubres, took their chief town, Taurasia, after a three-day siege. In the 1st century BCE the Romans founded Augusta Taurinorum, a town of about 5,000 inhabitants within high walls; its Porta Palatina is still preserved. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the town was held by the Heruli, Ostrogoths and Lombards, and passed to the Franks under Charlemagne in 773. The Counts of Savoy gained control after the marriage of Adelaide of Susa to Otto, son of Humbert Biancamano, and when the city was annexed to the Duchy of Savoy at the end of the 13th century it had 20,000 inhabitants.

Emmanuel Philibert, nicknamed Iron Head, made Turin the capital of the Duchy of Savoy in 1563. The French Empire annexed it with the rest of Piedmont in 1802, and in 1814 the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia was restored with Turin as its capital. That kingdom led the struggle for the unification of Italy, and Turin was the political and intellectual centre of the Risorgimento. It became the capital of the new Kingdom of Italy in 1861; the capital moved to Florence in 1865 and to Rome after the conquest of the Papal States in 1870.

Turin is the capital of Piedmont and is sometimes called the cradle of Italian liberty. Its architecture is predominantly Baroque, and part of the historical centre is inscribed in the World Heritage List as the Residences of the Royal House of Savoy. It is the base of Fiat, Lancia and Alfa Romeo, and hosted the 2006 Winter Olympics.
turkey: Turkey, officially the Republic of Türkiye, lies mainly in Anatolia, which makes up 97% of its surface, with a smaller part called East Thrace in Southeast Europe. Together they cover 783,562 square kilometres, and the Turkish straits and the Sea of Marmara run between them. The inland Anatolian Plateau grows more rugged towards the east, where Mount Ararat, the highest point at 5,137 metres, and Lake Van, the largest lake, are found. The Euphrates, the Tigris and the Aras rise in the east, and the country is divided into seven major regions.

The area has been inhabited by modern humans since the late Paleolithic and holds some of the oldest Neolithic sites, among them Göbekli Tepe, close to 12,000 years old, and Çatalhöyük. Written records begin with clay tablets of about 2000 BCE from Kültepe, which belonged to an Assyrian trade colony. The Hittite kingdom, with its capital at Hattusa, lasted approximately between 1700 and 1200 BCE, and Phrygia was established around 750 BCE. Alexander the Great's conquests brought Hellenization, followed by Romanization under the Roman and Byzantine empires.

The Seljuk Turks began migrating into Anatolia in the 11th century. The Seljuk Sultanate of Rum ruled until the Mongol invasion of 1243, after which Turkish principalities emerged. From 1299 the Ottomans united them, and Mehmed II conquered Constantinople in 1453. The Ottoman state entered World War I in 1914, and its government committed genocides against its Armenian, Greek and Assyrian subjects. After defeat came the Turkish War of Independence, the abolition of the sultanate and the Treaty of Lausanne. Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the founder and first president, proclaimed the Republic on 29 October 1923.

Turkey has more than 86 million people. Most are ethnic Turks, and Kurds are the largest minority, with estimates ranging from 12 to 20% of the population because census figures have not recorded ethnicity since 1965. Ankara is the capital and Istanbul the largest city. The country is a presidential republic under the constitution approved by referendum in 1982, with a 600-member Parliament and 81 provinces.
turku: Turku lies at the mouth of the Aura River in the south-western corner of Finland and covers both banks. The eastern bank, where Turku Cathedral stands, is the older and original centre; the western side, with Turku Castle, is the newer part. South-western Finland stayed below sea level for a long time after the Ice Age, and tectonic uplift turned the region from an outlying archipelago into a shoreline between about 3000 and 2000 BCE. In the Iron Age it was densely populated, and the word Finland once referred only to the area round Turku, which is why the province is called Finland Proper.

The Finnish name Turku is related to the word torg, meaning market. Pope Gregory IX mentioned the town of Aboa in his bull of 1229, and that year is now used as the founding year of the city. By the pope's permission of 23 January 1229 the episcopal seat was moved from Nousiainen to Koroinen, near the present centre. Because no reliable document records the founding, it has also been suggested that the city was founded in the 1280s or 1290s by the joint initiative of the king, the bishop and the Dominican Convent of Saint Olaf. Turku was the most important city in Finland under Swedish rule.

After the Finnish War, Sweden ceded Finland to Russia at the Treaty of Fredrikshamn in 1809, and the Russians entered Turku in October 1809 without resistance. Turku became the capital of the Grand Duchy of Finland but lost the status in 1812, when Emperor Alexander I decided to move the capital to Helsinki. After the last great fire, in 1827, most government institutions were moved to Helsinki together with the Royal Academy of Turku, founded in 1640, which later became the University of Helsinki.

Turku is the oldest city in Finland and the regional capital of Southwest Finland, with about 210,000 inhabitants. It is officially bilingual in Finnish and Swedish. The Swedish-language Åbo Akademi was founded there in 1918 and the Finnish-language University of Turku two years later. Its port runs ferries to Stockholm and Mariehamn.
tuva: Tuva lies at the geographical centre of Asia in southern Siberia, and its capital, Kyzyl, stands near the geographic centre of the continent. The republic is a mountain basin about 600 metres above sea level, encircled by the Sayan and Tannu-Ola ranges, and mountains and hills cover over 80 per cent of its territory. Its highest point is Mongun-Tayga, at 3,970 metres. There are over 8,000 rivers, including the upper course of the Yenisei. It borders Mongolia to the south.

The territory was controlled by a succession of powers, among them the Xiongnu, the Rouran Khaganate, the Tang dynasty, the Mongol Empire and the Yuan dynasty. From 1758 to 1911 Tuva was part of China's Qing dynasty, administered through Outer Mongolia. During the Xinhai Revolution of 1911 a separatist movement formed among the Tuvans, and on 17 April 1914 Tuva became a Russian protectorate as Uryankhay Krai. In 1918 and 1919 it was occupied by the White Russian troops of Alexander Kolchak, later by China, until the Bolsheviks expelled the Chinese in 1921.

On 14 August 1921 the Bolsheviks established the Tuvan People's Republic, popularly called Tannu-Tuva, formally independent between the World Wars. Its capital was renamed Kyzyl, meaning red, in 1926. A coup of 1929, carried out by five young Tuvans trained in Moscow, replaced Chairman Donduk Kuular, and Buddhist and Mongol influences were then curtailed. The Soviet Union annexed Tuva in 1944, with the approval of its Little Khural but without a referendum. Tuva signed the treaty creating the Russian Federation on 31 March 1992.

The Republic of Tyva is a republic of the Russian Federation, with 336,651 inhabitants at the 2021 census, more than a third of them in Kyzyl. Tuvans make up most of the population and speak the Tuvan language, a Turkic language. Tuvan and Russian are both official. Tuvan throat singing, in which the singer produces a fundamental tone and an overtone together, is a defining tradition. Tibetan Buddhism, first met in the 13th and 14th centuries, coexists with shamanism, which is preserved as part of traditional culture.
tycho-brahe: Tycho was born Tyge Ottesen Brahe on 14 December 1546 at his family's seat at Knutstorp in Scania, then Danish, the oldest of twelve siblings. He was heir to several of Denmark's most influential noble families, and both his grandfathers and all his great-grandfathers had served on the king's Privy Council. In 1566 he went to study at the University of Rostock. On 29 December of that year he lost part of his nose in a sword duel with his third cousin Manderup Parsberg, after a drunken quarrel over who was the better mathematician, and he wore a prosthetic nose for the rest of his life. His family had expected him to enter politics or law but supported his choice of the sciences.

Tycho devoted himself to more accurate instruments, enlarging the sextant and the quadrant, and mounted them underground on the bedrock once he realised that wind and the movement of buildings affected them. King Frederick II granted him an estate on Hven and money to build Uraniborg, the first large observatory in Christian Europe. In De nova stella of 1573 he refuted the Aristotelian belief in an unchanging celestial realm, and he showed that comets were not atmospheric phenomena. He could not reconcile Copernican heliocentrism with Aristotelian physics, so he devised a system in which the Sun and Moon orbit the Earth and the other planets orbit the Sun.

After Frederick's death in 1588 Tycho's influence at court declined, and in 1597 he was forced by the new king to leave Denmark. He was invited to Prague, where he became imperial astronomer and built an observatory at Benátky nad Jizerou.

Tycho fell ill after a banquet in Prague and died eleven days later, on 24 October 1601, aged 54. Before dying he urged Johannes Kepler to finish the Rudolphine Tables using Tycho's own planetary system. Kepler used Tycho's records of the motion of Mars to deduce his laws of planetary motion. Tycho's planetary model was soon discredited, but his observations were an essential contribution to the Scientific Revolution. Danish scholarship often depicted him as a mediocre scholar and a traitor to the nation, but from the second half of the 20th century scholars reassessed his significance.
